sources.news_title: UN head urges climate summit to act now
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for an "immediate and drastic reduction" in greenhouse gas emissions, as divisions over fossil fuels dominated the first week of COP31 climate talks in Turkey.
Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, observers said as the first week of talks drew to a close.
That poses a challenge for summit host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, which have another week to land the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates such as Guterres say is needed.
"The central question is in the hands of member states, particularly the big emitters. They must recognise the need for an immediate and drastic reduction in emissions to keep the 1.5 goal still possible by the end of the century," he said, referring to the warming limit countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A UN report last month found the world is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold, a limit scientists say should prevent the worst effects of climate change.
As temperatures have risen, this year has been marked by extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood that killed more than 1,450 people. Thousands more are still missing.
Major oil producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally resisted language constraining fossil fuels, while large developing economies such as India have opposed measures they say could limit their development and energy choices, a dynamic that has compromised the outcomes of past deals.
The world’s biggest oil consumer, the United States, meanwhile, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row under US President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
"We must confront the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby. The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction," said Guterres, who is leaving his job at the end of December after two five-year terms.
"But I remain hopeful. I've also seen something extraordinary over these 10 years. Renewable energy has moved from the margins to the mainstream. The economics have changed. The technology has advanced. A cleaner, safer, and more secure energy future is in our hands. The question is whether we have the courage and speed to reach for it."
Cop31 host Turkey is striving to place a proposal to expand global electrification at the centre of an eventual deal, saying the plan will lead to emissions cuts by speeding the shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars, boilers and other equipment.
The proposal does not require the increased electricity use to come from renewable sources, although some countries, including last year’s Cop host Brazil, are advocating for progress on a plan to require countries to more clearly map out their transition away from fossil fuels.
Katrine Petersen, an observer for the non-governmental organisation E3G, said whether those measures survive the talks depends on conversations in the days to come.
"We've also heard quite clearly from countries like India, the G77, that they don't want any firm targets. They don't want any kind of technology or fuel-specific language," she said. "(These are) the kind of consistent and ongoing divides that we've seen from those different parties before."
Representatives from India, Saudi Arabia and Russia did not immediately comment.
Diana Acconcia, head of the EU delegation, said Europe backed the electrification goal.
"Electrification is, in a way, an inclusive agenda because it is non-prescriptive in a way on how the electrification is achieved," she said. "Of course, for the European Union electrification is to be achieved by clean sources of energy."
The Australian team, which is leading negotiations under a split presidency arrangement, spent the first few days of the summit gathering views on what should be included in a political text agreed by consensus that will be followed by all the negotiated technical points.
Australia is taking further submissions from countries until Saturday night, with a view to formulating a draft text early next week. (Reuters)
Edited by Robert Kemp

sources.news_title: UN chief says ‘immediate and drastic’ emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe – WTOP News
sources.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — The world must immediately and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Friday at his final climate summit, urging the world to “follow the science” and face hard facts.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” Guterres told reporters, stressing that climate change is central to the U.N.’s work because it contributes to geopolitical instability by driving hunger and displacement, pushing countries into debt and fueling competition for land and water.
“You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it,” he added. “You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst.”
World leaders meeting in Turkey for the annual U.N. climate talks are trying to reach consensus on concrete actions to address climate change — which is fueling more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters — and help countries at greatest risk, including island nations that also are losing land to rising seas.
Electrification goals emerge as point of contention
Achieving reductions in emissions is setting up a point of contention at the climate talks, especially around electrification. A goal introduced this year would increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind.
But it does not require that electricity be generated by renewable sources — something Guterres said is essential — meaning coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially. Climate TRACE, which tracks global emissions via satellites, found that prioritizing clean energy would cut global emissions 14% compared to 7% if fossil fuels also are used for electrification.
International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol said it’s more important that as many countries as possible sign on to the pledge, which works best without a clean energy requirement.
But environmental groups say that electrification will only have a real impact if fossil fuels are omitted.
“Electrification must end fossil fuel dependence, not be an end in itself,” said Jasmin Duregger, from Greenpeace’s Global Gas Campaign.
Vulnerable nations seek more compensation as warming takes a toll
Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable countries that contributed little to the problem — also are calling for more money to deal with climate disasters and adapt to a warming world. Leaders of small island nations, who say climate change is a life-or-death matter for their people because rising seas are engulfing their lands, have been the most vocal at this year’s summit, COP31, saying a U.N. fund created for compensating vulnerable nations must be urgently strengthened.
Guterres said wealthier countries that have contributed most to climate change “must deliver the finance they have promised” at past summits — but also contribute much more.
“Let us be clear about the scale of the gap,” he said. “Even tripling adaptation finance would meet less than 30 percent of what is needed.”
Progress stalls, top-emitting countries skip summit
Progress is difficult without the cooperation of all nations, “particularly the biggest emitters,” Guterres said.
A report released Thursday by the independent Climate Action Tracker found that progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years. That means the world is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.
Climate change is caused primarily by greenhouse gases emitted by burning gas, oil and coal, and countries have established plans to reduce those emissions. But even if they fulfill all their promises — a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said.
“Our responsibility is to keep it as small as possible, for as short a time as possible and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as we can,” by cutting emissions about 6% per year for several years, Guterres said, calling the overshoot “a recipe for catastrophe.”
But some of the top-polluting countries stayed away from this year’s summit, most notably the United States — the world’s second-largest polluter after China and the largest historical polluter.
It’s the second year in a row the U.S. skipped the summit, after President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations.
“Facts are facts,” Guterres said. “No country can protect itself from climate change alone. We share one planet, and whether we like it or not, we share one fate.”
___
Webber reported from Fenton, Michigan; Borenstein from Kensington, Maryland; and Delgado from Bangkok.

sources.news_title: U.N. Leader Says People Power Is the Secret Weapon Against Global Warming
sources.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—Despite the lack of progress toward the goal of curbing global warming, outgoing U.N. Secretary General António Guterres urged climate activists and environmental justice advocates at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference here not to give up hope.
“You pushed governments to face up to the role of fossil fuels,” he said during his speech Friday to about 800 representatives of civil society groups from around the world. “You fought for finance for communities facing the worst impacts of a crisis they did little to cause. But let’s be clear. We face powerful lobbies that are pressuring governments. So civil society must put the needed counter-pressure against that.”
Guterres, former prime minister of Portugal, said a big part of the effort is to protect future generations who can’t influence today’s decisions. He said it’s essential to “do everything to make sure that those responsible for essential decisions create the conditions for a rapid, drastic reduction of emissions.”
While cutting carbon dioxide emissions is the only proven way to stop warming, this year’s Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, once again is far from addressing the issue of fossil fuels.
A voluntary global pledge to increase electrification holds the most promise for reducing emissions, but even that has become contentious, as some countries are resisting using the term “clean electrification,” which means producing electricity from renewables, rather than fossil fuels. Converting systems to run on electricity doesn’t reduce emissions if the electricity is produced by burning coal, oil or gas.
And there is a danger the U.N. process could backslide. Observers at some of the closed-door sessions this week said several countries, mainly Russia and Saudi Arabia, may be trying to block adoption of a final conference decision document—an outcome that could lead to the summit being widely perceived as a failure, even if such a text is not procedurally required.
All decisions and documents at the conference must be adopted by consensus, and Saudi Arabia’s 30-year history of obstructing efforts to address fossil fuels is well documented.
Guterres’s 10-year term as U.N. secretary-general ends Dec. 31. He has been outspoken about global warming and environmental justice. Even though international cooperation on climate and other issues has deteriorated recently, he has an abiding faith that collective action can overcome seemingly intractable social and political circumstances.
That belief, he has said, is rooted in part from his experiences during Portugal’s 1974 Carnation Revolution, when citizens arose against the country’s military dictatorship to establish what has become one of Europe’s most stable democracies.

“Secretary-General Guterres has been a tireless champion for climate action and a powerful voice for protecting our ocean and the communities that depend on it,” she said. “His unwavering belief that cooperation is possible, even in a deeply divided world, was the message many of us needed to hear.”

sources.news_title: UN chief warns of climate catastrophe as emission cuts lag
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for immediate, drastic cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, warning that a temporary breach of the 1.5°C global warming threshold is now inevitable.
Speaking at a news conference on the sidelines of the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye's southern city of Antalya on Friday, Guterres said global emissions must fall by around 6 percent annually over the next few years to limit the scale and duration of the overshoot.
“An overshoot of 1.5 degrees is now inevitable,” he said, stressing the need to keep it “as small as possible for as short a time as possible” and bring temperatures back below the threshold as quickly as possible.
He warned that current national climate commitments put the world on track for approximately 2.5°C of warming by the end of the century, describing the trajectory as “a recipe for catastrophe".
Guterres called for a faster, just and equitable transition away from fossil fuels, stressing that the expansion of renewable energy must be accompanied by reductions in fossil fuel production and consumption.
“Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis. There is no credible path to a safe climate without moving away from them,” he said.
He urged developed countries to honour their climate finance commitments and accelerate emissions reductions, while calling on emerging economies to speed up their transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
Guterres also emphasised the need for greater support for developing countries, particularly the most vulnerable, to help them adapt to the climate crisis and address loss and damage.

sources.news_title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
sources.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.
Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.
“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”
The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the UN “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.
“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”
Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

sources.news_title: Global economy anchored to a well-above-2°C warming trajectory
sources.text:
The global economy is increasingly anchored to a well-above-2°C warming trajectory, according to a report by risk intelligence organisation LSEG.
New research has found even though climate action is accelerating, it is not fast enough to meet the Paris Agreement’s temperature goals.
LSEG’s analysis shows that a decade after the Paris Agreement, accelerating climate action, stronger policy commitments and the rapid deployment of clean technologies have made the most extreme warming scenarios increasingly unlikely.
However it also shows that meeting countries’ current 2035 climate commitments and maintaining emissions at those levels would imply approximately 2.35°C of warming by 2100.
Continued reductions beyond 2035 could lower this to around 2.16°C, while faster progress towards net-zero commitments could reduce warming further to 2.08°C.
Jaakko Kooroshy, Global Head of Sustainable Investment Research at LSEG, said: “A decade after Paris, the energy transition has materially changed the outlook for global warming.
“Hot House scenarios, where warming exceeds 3°C or even 4°C, are looking increasingly unlikely, but the global economy appears increasingly anchored to a ‘well-above’ 2°C trajectory.”
The findings still show hazards such as heat and drought account for around 73% of the direct physical impact on global economic growth. Physical climate shocks can also spread through supply chains, trade and demand.

sources.news_title: World faces ‘irrecoverable overshoot’ on global warming without action
sources.text:
Current government policies put the world on track for 2.7C of warming by 2100, a report warns.

UN chief urges drastic emissions cuts as COP31 wrestles with fossil fuels
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 13 (Reuters) - UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for an "immediate and drastic reduction" in greenhouse gas emissions, as divisions over fossil fuels dominated the first week of COP31 climate talks in Turkey.
Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, observers said as the first week of talks drew to a close.
That poses a challenge for summit host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, which have another week to land the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates such as Guterres say is needed.
"The central question is in the hands of member states, particularly the big emitters. They must recognise the need for an immediate and drastic reduction in emissions to keep the 1.5 goal still possible by the end of the century," he said, referring to the warming limit countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A UN report last month found the world is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold, a limit scientists say should prevent the worst effects of climate change.
As temperatures have risen, this year has been marked by extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood that killed more than 1,450 people. Thousands more are still missing.
THE FOSSIL FUEL LOBBY
Major oil producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally resisted language constraining fossil fuels, while large developing economies such as India have opposed measures they say could limit their development and energy choices, a dynamic that has compromised the outcomes of past deals.
The world’s biggest oil consumer, the United States, meanwhile, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
"We must confront the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby. The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction," said Guterres, who is leaving his job at the end of December after two five-year terms.
"But I remain hopeful. I've also seen something extraordinary over these 10 years. Renewable energy has moved from the margins to the mainstream. The economics have changed. The technology has advanced. A cleaner, safer, and more secure energy future is in our hands. The question is whether we have the courage and speed to reach for it."
ELECTRIFICATION AND NO FIRM TARGETS
COP31 host Turkey is striving to place a proposal to expand global electrification at the centre of an eventual deal, saying the plan will lead to emissions cuts by speeding the shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars, boilers and other equipment.
The proposal does not require the increased electricity use to come from renewable sources, although some countries, including last year’s COP host Brazil, are advocating for progress on a plan to require countries to more clearly map out their transition away from fossil fuels.
Katrine Petersen, an observer for the non-governmental organisation E3G, said whether those measures survive the talks depends on conversations in the days to come.
"We've also heard quite clearly from countries like India, the G77, that they don't want any firm targets. They don't want any kind of technology or fuel-specific language," she said. "(These are) the kind of consistent and ongoing divides that we've seen from those different parties before."
Representatives from India, Saudi Arabia and Russia did not immediately comment.
Diana Acconcia, head of the EU delegation, said Europe backed the electrification goal.
"Electrification is, in a way, an inclusive agenda because it is non-prescriptive in a way on how the electrification is achieved," she said. "Of course, for the European Union electrification is to be achieved by clean sources of energy."
The Australian team, which is leading negotiations under a split presidency arrangement, spent the first few days of the summit gathering views on what should be included in a political text agreed by consensus that will be followed by all the negotiated technical points.
Australia is taking further submissions from countries until Saturday night, with a view to formulating a draft text early next week.
(Reporting by William James, Sarah McFarlane, Valerie Volcovici, Simon Jessop and Richard Valdmanis; editing by Barbara Lewis)

sources.news_title: Report warns world headed for ‘irrecoverable’ climate overshoot
sources.text:
The world is heading toward an "irrecoverable overshoot" of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5-degree Celsius warming limit after five years in which progress on climate action was canceled out by setbacks, Climate Action Tracker (CAT) warned Thursday.
The independent monitoring group said unfulfilled plans and offsetting actions had left projected warming unchanged, despite a new round of national climate commitments submitted last year.
"Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions canceling each other out," the report said.
The assessment, released during a U.N. climate meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, contrasted the recent stagnation with progress during the first five years after the 2015 Paris Agreement.
Action during that earlier period lowered projected warming by an entire degree Celsius, or 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the report.
Since then, collective efforts have failed to significantly reduce global greenhouse gas emissions, leaving the world "headed toward an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius" above preindustrial temperatures.
Even if countries fulfill all their climate promises, the report projects warming of 2.6 degrees Celsius by the end of the century. That is the same outlook as in 2024 and 2025.
The latest national pledges have therefore failed to change the projected warming trajectory, said lead author Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst at CAT.
"This is still not enough," Heck said. "Countries really do need to strengthen their targets."
Countries set out their emissions reduction plans in commitments known as nationally determined contributions. Those plans differ in the speed and scale of proposed cuts and the measures governments intend to use.
But pledges must translate into substantial reductions in emissions, primarily from burning coal, oil and gas, to slow warming. The report’s warning underscored the gap between countries’ stated ambitions and their combined impact.
For island nations, exceeding the 1.5-degree limit threatens to compound dangers already evident in rising seas, damaged coral reefs and increasingly destructive extreme weather.
Leaders from those countries urged stronger action Wednesday, with more expected to address the Antalya meeting Thursday.
"Every new oil well drilled, every piece of coal extracted is a threat to my country’s future. The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate, but something to fear," Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine said Wednesday.
"No one has the right to pollute their neighbors."
Heine described watching coral change from "bright and lush" to white as it bleached this year. She said the global response to the inevitability of exceeding the 1.5-degree limit "must be overwhelming or the world we know is over."
"It is time to wake up," she said.
Leaders from Tuvalu, the Bahamas, Antigua and Barbuda, Niue and other island nations were expected to make similar appeals Thursday.
Alongside the worsening heat waves, storms, droughts and floods affecting countries worldwide, island nations face rising seas that threaten to swallow their land.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley said Wednesday that wealthy nations must deliver more funding to help poorer countries recover from climate damage and adapt to a warmer world.
"Pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels," Mottley told fellow leaders.
"So the applause in this room, let us be clear, has never rebuilt a single home in any country," she added.

Fossil fuels are ‘killing our planet,’ UN chief warns at climate talks
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
ANTALYA, Turkey — Opening a climate summit that leaders from most industrialized nations chose to skip, António Guterres, the United Nations secretary-general, on Wednesday warned that the planet was on a “path to mutually assured destruction,” unable to wean itself from planet-warming fossil fuels and facing intensifying disasters.
“Fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet,” Guterres told world leaders gathering for the summit, known as COP31.
Guterres, who is in the final weeks of his term after leading the United Nations for a decade, urged nations to “end the addiction” to fossil fuels. His remarks sharpened the tensions for an event that often struggles to directly address the burning of fossil fuels, which is the root cause of climate change.
He and others acknowledged that the world has failed to meet the goal it established in the Paris Agreement in 2015 to limit rising global temperatures to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels. That’s the threshold beyond which scientists say the dangers of global warming — including worsening floods, fiercer wildfires, droughts and ecosystem collapse — grow considerably.
On Wednesday, leaders one by one insisted that despite rising levels of greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere, it was critical to get back on track. But many avoided mentioning the cuts to coal, oil and gas that would be necessary to meet most climate goals.
“It is time to wake up,” said President Hilda Heine of the Marshall Islands, who described rising sea levels threatening her Pacific atoll nation.
“Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world that we know is over,” she said.
The two-day leaders’ summit is part of the broader U.N. climate conference, which began Monday in Antalya on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast. This year, 102 world leaders are attending, according to organizers, down from 156 three years ago.
At the same time, more than 92,000 people have registered to attend the summit, according to the U.N., making it the largest climate conference in history.
COP31 comes at a challenging time for climate efforts. Wars and tariffs have driven a wedge into international cooperation. The U.S. and Israeli fight against Iran, now in its ninth month, has disrupted the flow of oil from the Middle East and pushed up global fuel prices. Nations are building up solar and wind capacity as a hedge against shocks while also burning more coal to ensure a stable energy supply. And in part because of data centers to power artificial intelligence, nations need more energy than ever — whatever the source.
In the consensus-based U.N. climate talks, even a single nation can upend an agreement, one reason why it has been difficult for nations to implement an earlier pledge to move away from fossil fuels.
As if highlighting the fight to come, Saudi Arabia’s energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, said that cutting emissions could happen through “available techniques,” and emphasized the importance of “maintaining energy security.”
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil said climate change had “disappeared” from the global stage over the past two years.
Without directly mentioning the United States or President Donald Trump, who has imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian products, he said, “We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations.”
The United States, the largest historic emitter of greenhouse gases, withdrew from the Paris climate agreement and is no longer working to reduce carbon emissions. Beyond Trump, the list of leaders skipping the summit is long: President Xi Jinping of China, Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, President Vladimir Putin of Russia and President Prabowo Subianto of Indonesia. They represent the five nations that emit the most annual emissions.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain, who is scheduled to speak Thursday, was expected to be the only leader of the Group of 7 wealthy nations to attend the climate summit.
“It really is a disgrace,” Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate research group, said in a statement. “The world’s biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others.”
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, attended the summit, as did Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, who called for the “free flow of green technology” — a reference to trade barriers amid China’s clean energy dominance.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey used his address to call for more humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip. He referred to the war between Israel and Hamas militants that began in 2023 as “not only a genocide, but an ecocide.”
The war, Erdogan said, had uprooted olive trees, polluted the soil and water in the seaside territory and turned Gaza’s cities into “enormous piles of rubble.”
Israel strongly rejects any suggestion that it committed genocide. Erdogan has often harshly criticized Israel and its treatment of Palestinians, contributing to increasingly tense relations between Turkey and Israel.
Israel did not send anyone to the conference, according to a provisional list of delegates published by the U.N. climate body.
Several leaders on Wednesday detailed how climate change was upending their nations, with Iraqi President Nizar Amedi saying that water scarcity was jeopardizing “societal stability” in a cradle of civilization. Heine, of the Marshall Islands, described seeing “bright and lush” coral reef on her home island in July; months later it had been bleached white.
“We are watching ecosystems die,” she said.
Andrea Woods, a spokesperson for the American Petroleum Institute, the main oil and gas lobbying group in the United States, said the industry has significantly reduced emissions since 2015.
“Rather than restricting the infrastructure needed to meet growing energy demand, policymakers should be focused on practical solutions that build on this progress and strengthen global energy security,” she said.
In his speech, Guterres called out fossil fuel interests several times and drew applause when he said, “I will not stop telling the truth.”
Nations agreed three years ago to transition away from fossil fuels, starting with steps this decade. But some oil- and gas-exporting countries have since ramped up production. Carbon emissions continue to rise. Countries such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked recent U.N. conferences from revisiting the deal and fleshing out specifics.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” Guterres said. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do.”

sources.news_title: World faces 'irrecoverable overshoot' on warming
sources.text:
The world is heading for an "irrecoverable overshoot" on dangerous warming unless governments reject fossil fuels and start rapidly cutting emissions, a report has warned.
The latest update from the Climate Action Tracker (CAT) initiative, released as countries meet for COP31, United Nations climate talks in Turkey, warns that collective climate action has stalled for the fifth consecutive year.
There are positive signs, with clean electricity meeting all additional global demand for power in 2025, China and India deploying renewables at a record pace, electric vehicle roll out reaching new highs, and deforestation in the Amazon falling sharply.
However, the report warns that progress on deploying alternatives to fossil fuels - which cause most of the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming when they are burned for transport, heating, power and industry - is not happening fast enough.
Increasing demand for energy and new fossil fuel infrastructure being built have led to still rising emissions, the CAT warns.
It finds that, with the policies on tackling climate change and driving clean energy and technologies that governments have in place today, the world is on track for 2.7C of warming by 2100 - up slightly from 2.6C last year and the same as 2021 to 2024.
If governments met 2030 and 2035 targets to cut emissions under the Paris Agreement - a global treaty that aims to curb warming to 1.5C to avoid the most dangerous impacts of climate change - it would still be 2.6C, the same as last year.
Under an optimistic scenario, in which countries meet all of their pledges and targets to cut emissions to zero overall, the world would see warming of 1.9C by the end of the century.
The Paris target - of 1.5C - is set to be exceeded in the next few years, and experts warn there is a need to act to limit the size and duration of the overshoot, and bring temperatures down to below 1.5C above pre-industrial temperatures by 2100.
Chief Executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics Bill Hare said: "The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases, and disasters that they are unable to adapt to, or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever.
"The imminence of breaching 1.5C cannot be an excuse to open the door to defeatism - the focus has to be on accelerating action to limit the magnitude and duration of overshoot.
"Every increment of warming above 1.5C means even more significant consequences across climate, nature and human systems."
Scientists warn that exceeding 1.5C of global warming will lead to more severe weather extremes such as deadly heatwaves, floods, storms and drought, rising sea levels, and the potential for catastrophic and irreversible collapse of natural systems, such as coral reefs and rainforests.
Analysis published earlier this week by the Global Carbon Budget initiative suggested a slight decline in carbon emissions from fossil fuels this year, of 0.4%, driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict.
Dr Niklas Hohne, of CAT partner organisation NewClimate Institute, said: "With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz exposing our vulnerability to geopolitical shocks, the case for renewables and electrification has never been stronger.
"It does appear that global emissions could be on the verge of a peak and a much faster decline than we had previously thought."

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.
“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.
“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”
The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”
“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”
Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”
Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.
In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”
Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.
The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.
Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.
Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.
“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”
world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”
Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

sources.news_title: UN Chief at COP31: Climate Crisis 'Is Outrunning Us'
sources.text:
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders on Wednesday that the slow international response to climate change has put the world on "the path to mutually assured destruction," opening a two-day leaders' summit at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. "The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said.
Guterres pointed to a set of markers. Emissions reached an all-time high in 2025, he said, heat records "keep shattering," and the last four years were the hottest ever recorded. Climate disasters, he said, are "pounding lives, livelihoods and economies across the globe." He added that the science was not a reason to give up. "It is telling us to fight harder," he said.
Guterres also said that the goal at the center of a decade of climate negotiations will be missed, at least for a time. He said an overshoot of the 1.5-degree Celsius limit set in the 2015 Paris Agreement "is now inevitable," but argued that governments can still decide how large and how long the breach will be. "We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach," he said. Leaders including Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged in their own remarks that warming can no longer be held below that limit. It was Guterres's last climate conference as secretary-general.
He directed some of his sharpest language at the oil, gas and coal industry, accusing the fossil fuel lobby of delaying climate action. "Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won't happen on its own," Guterres said. "The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do." He said fossil fuel interests "keep making a killing, while killing our planet," and called on leaders to work toward ending the use of coal, gas and oil as energy sources.
The conference, the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, opened Monday at the Antalya Expo Center on Turkey's Mediterranean coast and runs through Nov. 20. It is being held under an unusual arrangement in which Turkey is the host and Australia leads the negotiations. Turkey's environment minister, Murat Kurum, presides over the conference. The leaders' segment on Wednesday and Thursday is meant to give political direction to the technical talks that follow.
The list of those attending says as much as the speeches. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is hosting, and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed are among the leaders present, along with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. China sent Vice President Han Zheng. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is due to speak Thursday, is the only leader of a Group of Seven country taking part. France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada did not send their top leaders. The United States sent no official delegation for the second year in a row, after President Donald Trump withdrew the country from international climate cooperation. Together with China and India, whose top leaders also stayed away, it accounts for more than half of global carbon dioxide emissions. More than 70 leaders were due to speak over the two days.
Erdogan said the world must ensure it is heading toward a future in which energy is clean, reliable and affordable and economies are strong. Han, speaking through a translator, stressed the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, the long-standing position of developing countries that wealthier nations should bear more of the burden. He told Guterres that China was committed to setting clear targets and carrying them out.
Lula, who was re-elected last month and whose country hosted last year's conference in Belem, said the issue had slipped down the global agenda. "We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations," he said. He urged the hosts to give priority to climate finance, to the move away from fossil fuels and to the deforestation goals taken up in Belem.
Leaders from poorer countries pressed the question of money. Abiy said faster emissions cuts were needed to make the future affordable, and that those with the greatest responsibility and means should lead with deeper cuts this decade. "We cannot be expected to borrow our way out of a crisis we did little to create," he said, adding that resilience must not come at the cost of unsustainable debt. Chris Bowen, the Australian climate and energy minister who is leading the negotiations, told leaders that just 0.2% of climate finance goes to small island developing states to help them adapt.
Pezeshkian used his speech to connect the climate agenda to the war with the United States and Israel. Speaking through a translator, he called on the international community to link climate commitments in peacetime with responsibility in wartime, to document and assess the environmental damage caused by military attacks, and to develop mechanisms for compensation. His presence in Antalya, alongside the emir of Qatar, which has been mediating between Tehran and Washington, put the conflict on the margins of a summit that was not convened to discuss it.
The summit is taking place against a crowded political backdrop. Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, high inflation and fiscal pressures have competed for governments' attention, and the absence of most leaders of the largest developed economies reflects that. The war with Iran has driven up prices for oil, gasoline and products such as fertilizer, and has prompted governments to rethink their energy policies, including investment in wind and solar power.
Organizers have framed this year's conference around delivery. Laurent Fabius, the former French prime minister who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and now leads an advisory council of former summit presidents, said the leaders' speeches should give political impetus to the negotiations. "The key word in Antalya is implementation," he said, describing the summit as an opportunity for leaders to explain how they will carry out the commitments they have already made.
Not everyone is persuaded that the annual conferences can deliver. The climate activist Greta Thunberg criticized the summits this week as being full of industry lobbyists, saying that "everything we love is at stake." Her criticism echoed Guterres's own remarks about the influence of fossil fuel interests, though from outside the process he is trying to defend.
The test of the conference will come in its second week, after the leaders have left. Negotiators are expected to work on how countries will meet existing emissions targets and how adaptation in poorer countries will be financed, the two areas where past summits have produced pledges that were only partly met. Whether Antalya ends with measurable commitments or with another statement of intent will be clear when the talks close on Nov. 20.

sources.news_title: COP31: Guterres faults fossil fuel lobby, demands $1.3tn for developing countries
sources.text:
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has called on developed countries and international financial institutions to mobilise at least $1.3 trillion annually for developing countries by 2035, warning that the global response to climate change is falling far behind the scale of the crisis.
Mr Guterres said climate finance commitments must translate into accessible funding for countries struggling to adapt to rising temperatures, build resilient infrastructure and transition to cleaner energy sources.
He also demanded an accelerated transition away from fossil fuels, accusing powerful industry interests of obstructing climate action while continuing to profit from activities contributing to global warming.
Mr Guterres made the demands on Wednesday at the World Leaders Summit of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, where heads of state and government gathered to discuss the implementation of international climate commitments.
|  |  | 
|---|---|
He said global emissions needed to decline by about six per cent annually, arguing that existing national climate plans, even if fully implemented, would deliver only about a third of the required reductions.
“Our first climate duty is to tell the truth. The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. Emissions in 2025 reached all-time highs. Heat records keep shattering. The last four years were the hottest ever,” he said.
Climate finance gap
Mr Guterres’ demand comes amid continuing concerns over the availability and accessibility of climate finance for developing countries, many of which face high costs in responding to extreme weather, protecting vulnerable communities and reducing emissions.

The $1.3 trillion annual financing ambition is not an entirely new commitment. It builds on the climate finance agreement reached at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, which established a goal of mobilising at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, led by developed countries, alongside a broader call to scale up funding from all sources to at least $1.3 trillion annually by the same year.
However, Mr Guterres said the wider financing ambition must move beyond political declarations to become actual funding available to countries that need it.
“Developed countries must lead in delivering at least $300 billion a year by 2035, and set out concrete plans with clear milestones to at least triple adaptation finance by then”.
“The $1.3 trillion goal must become real finance flowing to developing countries, and this demands that every source of finance pull its weight,” he said.
He noted that emerging and developing economies outside China account for nearly two-thirds of the world’s population but receive less than one-fifth of global clean energy investments.
He added that many of these countries pay two to three times more to borrow, making it difficult to finance renewable energy projects and climate adaptation programmes.
According to him, the disparity risks deepening dependence on fossil fuels, as countries unable to secure affordable clean-energy financing may continue investing in conventional energy infrastructure.
He called for greater contributions from multilateral development banks, private investors and donor countries, including more favourable lending arrangements and innovative financing instruments.
He also urged governments to strengthen funding for the Green Climate Fund and the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which supports vulnerable countries dealing with the consequences of climate-related disasters.
Fossil fuel industry under scrutiny
Beyond financing, Mr Guterres criticised the influence of fossil fuel companies on climate policy, arguing that the industry’s lobbying activities were slowing the transition to renewable energy.
He said the world could no longer justify continued dependence on coal, oil and gas when the economic and environmental costs of their use were becoming increasingly apparent.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” he said.
He accused fossil fuel interests of distorting scientific evidence, delaying policy decisions and avoiding accountability for environmental damage.
He argued that renewable energy had become increasingly competitive, noting that solar power, which accounted for only one per cent of global electricity generation a decade ago, met nearly three-quarters of the growth in electricity demand in the previous year.
He also cited the growing adoption of electric vehicles, saying nearly one in three new cars sold globally was expected to be electric in 2026.
Mr Guterres said three-quarters of the world’s population live in countries that import fossil fuels, leaving them vulnerable to international price fluctuations and energy insecurity.
He called for a just and orderly transition that would include ending new unabated coal development, reducing methane emissions and expanding electricity grids, energy storage and clean electrification.
He also urged governments to tax windfall profits made by fossil fuel companies and direct the proceeds towards countries affected by climate disasters.
Citing the financial disparity between oil companies and climate-vulnerable countries, he said the nine largest oil companies made $95 billion in profits in the last quarter, while the Loss and Damage Fund had received approximately $600 million.
“That is what these companies made in about 14 hours,” he said.
Leaders seek stronger climate action
The COP31 World Leaders Summit, taking place on 11 and 12 November, is part of the conference’s high-level discussions, which run from 9 to 20 November in Antalya.
The conference is being hosted by Türkiye, while Australia is leading the formal negotiations under an agreed partnership arrangement.
Other leaders at the summit also called for increased climate financing and practical interventions to protect vulnerable countries.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the growing threat of rising sea levels to Pacific island nations, particularly Tuvalu, where the average elevation of the islands is approximately 1.83 metres above sea level.
He recounted meeting a 13-year-old student in the country who feared for the future of her home, despite aspiring to become a doctor.
Reading her message to world leaders, Mr Albanese said the student was asking for international cooperation to protect communities threatened by rising oceans.

He said Australia had doubled its renewable electricity generation over six years, with renewables now accounting for half of the country’s electricity mix. He also disclosed that more than 600,000 home batteries had been installed in the country in the past year.
Meanwhile, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed called for climate action to be integrated into economic development planning, particularly in countries where changing weather patterns threaten agriculture and livelihoods.
“In Ethiopia, climate action is economic policy,” he said.
Mr Abiy said more than 90 per cent of Ethiopia’s electricity came from hydropower, while the country was expanding investments in wind, solar and geothermal energy.
He also highlighted Ethiopia’s Green Legacy Initiative, through which more than 56 billion seedlings had been planted to restore degraded land and expand forest cover.
He said climate financing must be predictable and accessible early enough to enable vulnerable countries to prepare for extreme weather events.
He urged international financiers to make their commitments measurable, asking them to specify the amount of funding available, when it would be delivered, and the conditions attached.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” said UN Secretary-General António Guterres.
At his last United Nations Climate Change Conference as secretary-general, António Guterres on Wednesday emphasized that he "will not stop telling the truth" about how the fossil fuel industry and the wealthy governments that continue to hand out oil and gas subsidies are allowing the sector to reap massive profits while people around the world suffer from the worsening impacts of the climate emergency.
“The last four years were the hottest ever, and fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet," the secretary-general said bluntly.
"Climate disasters are pounding lives, livelihoods, and economies across the globe," he added. "This is the path to mutually assured destruction."
Guterres spoke two days after the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) released its "State of the Climate" report at the conference, known as COP31, which is being hosted by the Turkish government in Antalya this year. The report warned that while the past 12 years have been the Earth's warmest on record, the trend has particularly accelerated since 2022.
The impacts have been brutal, with more than 1,500 people killed this year in Nepal and Tibet after a glacier collapsed and caused sudden catastrophic flooding, an estimated 200,000 people killed across Europe by extreme heat over the past years, and tens of thousands of acres scorched by wildfires across Europe and in the COP31 host country this summer.
Last month, the UN released a report finding that avoiding a global temperature rise over 1.5°C above preindustrial temperatures is no longer possible. Experts now say governments must work toward a goal of ensuring that the overshoot is only temporary, just over a decade after the warming limit was agreed to in the Paris Agreement at COP21.
On Wednesday, Guterres emphasized that the failure to avoid passing the 1.5°C limit comes as planet-warming emissions from the oil, gas, and coal industries have continued climbing—and as already wealthy companies' profits have soared.
Meanwhile, those same companies have spent hundreds of millions of dollars on lobbying in an effort to delay a transition away from fossil fuels and toward renewable energy sources.
“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," said Guterres Wednesday. "Emissions in 2025 reached all-time highs. Heat records keep shattering."
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs," he added. "And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do. And their strategy is simple: Distort the science. Delay policy. Delay action. Delay accountability.”
Guterres called on governments to tax oil and gas companies' windfall profits, like those the industry has reported since US President Donald Trump joined Israel in launching an illegal war in Iran. Since the conflict began in February, global energy prices have soared.
Last month, ExxonMobil reported $17.5 billion in adjusted earnings for the third quarter of 2026, while Chevron reported $10.4 billion. British company Shell earned $10.8 billion from July-September, and the French firm TotalEnergies brought in $9.1 billion.
The companies have reaped profits while the global Loss and Damage Fund, which experts and developing countries say needs about $400 billion annually from wealthier governments in order to help poorer countries adapt to emergency and repair damages, is woefully underfunded.
“Those who profit most from fossil fuels must help foot the bill for the damage they have caused," said Guterres. "In the last quarter alone, the nine largest oil companies pocketed $95 billion in profits. Meanwhile, the Loss and Damage Fund has received around $600 million. That is what these companies made in about 14 hours. It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits—and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”
David Tong, industry campaign manager for the global group Oil Change International (OCI), said in a statement that "trusting big oil to solve the climate crisis is like trusting big tobacco to cure lung cancer."
"Fossil fuel companies actively undermine a renewable energy future while trying to wring as much profits as possible out of fossil fuels while cashing in on conflict," said Tong. "It’s time to tax fossil fuel companies’ superprofits to pay for a transition to publicly owned renewable energy, governments must cut ties with fossil fuel companies and limit their influence on politics, and we must hold polluters accountable—legally and otherwise—for the damages they cause.”
OCI noted that Guterres' speech came shortly after YouGov released new polling that showed significant support in countries with large fossil fuel industries—the US, the UK, and France—for laws to phase out oil, gas, and coal production.
The climate action group 350.org said world leaders at COP31 must "turn growing international support for moving away from fossil fuels into a clear commitment at COP31."
Türkiye and Australia, which is serving as co-president of COP31, "will be to blame if this opportunity is allowed to slip away," said 350.org.
On Tuesday, said the group, attendees took part in "high-level events on roadmaps for transitioning away from fossil fuels," which "saw strong support from countries across negotiating blocs, alongside UN Secretary-General António Guterres, former COP presidents and ministers, for continuing the initiative launched by Brazil's COP30 Presidency in Belém last year."
"While Türkiye indicated it was open to considering the initiative, Australia offered no clear pathway for taking it forward," the organization continued.
Fenton Lutunatabua, Pacific and Caribbean program manager at 350.org, said that "the political mandate for a just and equitable transition away from fossil fuels is there."
"The world cannot afford another COP where governments acknowledge the need to move beyond fossil fuels but fail to agree on how to make it happen," said Lutunatabua. “If Australia is unwilling to advance this agenda, Türkiye must lead rather than allow one of the world's most fossil-fuel-dependent governments to hold back progress. The political support is there. What is missing is the leadership to turn it into action.”
This year's UN conference marks the second consecutive year without an official delegation from the US, the largest historic emitter of greenhouse gases, as Trump has refused to participate.
French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are also skipping the summit, leaving UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only G7 leader attending.
“It really is a disgrace,” Mohamed Adow, the director of Power Shift Africa, told The New York Times of the absences. “The world’s biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others.”
But Guterres stressed that despite the absence of leadership from the world's wealthiest economies, "science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder.”

sources.news_title: COP31: UN chief demands $1.3tn finance for developing countries
sources.text:
The United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has warned that the world is running out of time to contain the climate crisis.
Guterres called for an accelerated transition from fossil fuels, increased climate financing and urgent action to protect vulnerable countries from worsening global warming.
The Secretary-General on Wednesday said global emissions needed to decline by approximately six per cent annually, warning that existing national climate commitments were insufficient to prevent dangerous temperature increases, despite growing investments in renewable energy.
He urged developed countries to deliver at least $300bn annually in climate finance by 2035, ensuring that the wider $1.3tn financing ambition translated into actual funding for developing countries that are still working to improve their industrial capacity, infrastructure, income levels, healthcare, education and living standards.
He stated, “Developed countries must lead in delivering at least $300 billion a year by 2035, and set out concrete plans with clear milestones to at least triple adaptation finance by then.
“The $1.3tn goal must become real finance flowing to developing countries and this demands that every source of finance pull its weight.”
Guterres spoke at the World Leaders Summit of the ongoing 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye, where Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed also called for stronger international cooperation, climate financing and practical interventions to address the crisis.
The World Leaders Summit at COP31 brings together heads of state and government, alongside senior international officials, to discuss urgent climate challenges, strengthen global cooperation and translate climate commitments into concrete action.
The summit, attended by our correspondent, opened with a 30-minute cultural performance celebrating Türkiye’s heritage, featuring the renowned Fire of Anatolia dance ensemble.
The performance brought together traditional folk dances, music, colourful costumes and contemporary choreography to portray the historical meeting of civilisations in Anatolia.
The presentation reflected the region’s position as a historical crossroads between Europe and Asia, where different cultures, trade routes and civilisations have interacted over centuries.
The Fire of Anatolia, established in 1999, is known for combining traditional Anatolian folk dances with ballet and modern dance to promote cultural unity and peace.
The cultural display provided an opening message of coexistence and cooperation ahead of the leaders’ discussions on a climate crisis that increasingly requires countries to work across political and economic differences.
Addressing the summit, Guterres said the world must confront the reality that climate change was advancing faster than governments’ responses.
“Our first climate duty is to tell the truth. The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. Emissions in 2025 reached all-time highs. Heat records keep shattering. The last four years were the hottest ever,” he said.
He criticised fossil fuel interests for continuing to profit from activities contributing to global warming, warning that climate disasters were increasingly destroying lives, livelihoods and economies.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” Guterres said in Turkey at his final UN climate summit as secretary-general.
He recalled that countries had pledged under the 2015 Paris Agreement to limit global temperature increases to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, but said scientific evidence suggested that a temporary overshoot was now inevitable.
However, he argued that the prospect of exceeding the target should not become an excuse for inaction.
“Science tells us an overshoot above that level is now inevitable. But science is not telling us to surrender. It’s telling us to fight harder.
“The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be. We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach, not a permanent sentence,” he said.
The UN chief identified three major lessons from the past decade, including the rapid growth of renewable energy, the declining economic case for fossil fuels and the slow pace of global climate action.
He noted that solar energy, which accounted for only one per cent of global electricity generation a decade ago, had become a major contributor to meeting rising electricity demand, while electric vehicles were also gaining market share.
He said three-quarters of humanity lived in countries importing fossil fuels, leaving them exposed to international price shocks and energy insecurity.
“The case for fossil fuels is collapsing. Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels. Hostage to price shocks they did not create and they cannot control,” he said.
Guterres called for a just and orderly transition to renewable energy, including ending new coal development, reducing methane emissions and expanding electricity grids, energy storage and clean electrification.
He also demanded a new climate justice compact, arguing that developing countries were being denied the financial resources needed to implement climate commitments.
He said emerging and developing economies outside China accounted for nearly two-thirds of the world’s population but received less than one-fifth of global clean energy investments, while borrowing costs in many of those countries were two to three times higher.
He also criticised the imbalance between profits made by oil companies and resources available to countries suffering climate-related losses.
“In the last quarter alone, the nine largest oil companies pocketed $95bn in profits. Meanwhile, the Loss and Damage Fund has received around $600m. That is what these companies made in about 14 hours,” he said, calling for taxes on windfall profits from fossil fuel companies to support vulnerable countries.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who is leading the COP31 negotiations alongside Türkiye’s hosting arrangement, said the conference must translate climate commitments into practical results, particularly for Pacific island countries threatened by rising sea levels.
He recalled meeting a 13-year-old student, Melalusi Soketia, in Tuvalu, who feared for the future of her home despite dreaming of becoming a doctor.
Reading her message to world leaders, Albanese said, “We all have one simple dream, to grow up safely here in Tuvalu, the place we call home. We are not asking for pity, we are asking for help and partnership. Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”
He said the average elevation of Tuvalu’s islands was just 1.83 metres above sea level, making coastal communities particularly vulnerable to storm surges and rising oceans.
Albanese said Australia had doubled renewable electricity generation in six years, with renewables now accounting for half of its electricity mix.
He also disclosed that more than 600,000 home batteries had been installed in the country in the past year.
He called for increased investment in clean energy, electrification, ocean protection and climate adaptation, particularly for vulnerable countries.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, whose country is expected to host COP32 in 2027, said climate action must be treated as an economic development priority rather than an environmental commitment alone.
He explained that droughts and floods associated with changing weather patterns were affecting agricultural production, displacing families and threatening livelihoods in Ethiopia.
He said, “In Ethiopia, climate action is economic policy.”
Abiy disclosed that more than 90 per cent of Ethiopia’s electricity came from hydropower, making climate resilience and diversification of energy sources critical to its economic stability.
He said the country was expanding wind, solar and geothermal power while using satellite technology and artificial intelligence to improve weather forecasting and provide farmers with early warnings.
The Ethiopian leader also highlighted the country’s Green Legacy Initiative, through which more than 56 billion seedlings had been planted to restore degraded land, expand forests and create employment.
He said Ethiopia had banned imports of petrol- and diesel-powered cars as part of its transition to electric mobility, adding that climate financing must be released early enough to help vulnerable communities prepare for extreme weather.
On Ethiopia’s preparations to host COP32, he challenged international financiers to make their commitments measurable.
“That work should begin here, with every Pledge of Finance answering three questions. How much? By when? On what terms? The answers must be clear enough for a government to budget, an investor to commit, and a community to prepare,” he said.

sources.news_title: UN chief urges drastic emissions cuts
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for an “immediate and drastic reduction” in greenhouse gas emissions, as divisions over fossil fuels dominated the first week of COP31 climate talks in Turkey.
Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, observers said as the first week of talks drew to a close.
That poses a challenge for summit host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, which have another week to land the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates such as Guterres say is needed.
“The central question is in the hands of member states, particularly the big emitters.
They must recognise the need for an immediate and drastic reduction in emissions to keep the 1.5 goal still possible by the end of the century,” he said, referring to the warming limit countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A UN report last month found the world is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold, a limit scientists say should prevent the worst effects of climate change.
As temperatures have risen, this year has been marked by extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood that killed more than 1,450 people.
Thousands more are still missing.
Major oil producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally resisted language constraining fossil fuels, while large developing economies such as India have opposed measures they say could limit their development and energy choices, a dynamic that has compromised the outcomes of past deals.
The world’s biggest oil consumer, the United States, meanwhile, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
“We must confront the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby.
The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction,” said Guterres, who is leaving his job at the end of December after two five-year terms.
But I remain hopeful. I’ve also seen something extraordinary over these 10 years. Renewable energy has moved from the margins to the mainstream.
The economics have changed. The technology has advanced. A cleaner, safer, and more secure energy future is in our hands. The question is whether we have the courage and speed to reach for it.”

sources.news_title: Guterres Condemns Soaring Fossil Fuel Profits as ‘Morally Unacceptable’
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Thursday slammed soaring fossil fuel profits as “morally unacceptable” and demanded governments put their people ahead of the bottom lines of oil and gas giants.
In an exclusive interview with AFP at COP31, the outgoing UN chief said no country could pursue new fossil fuels while claiming to fight climate change — including summit organisers Turkey and Australia.
The climate conference in Antalya has resurfaced old fault lines over fossil fuels, with some countries pushing for a faster exit from coal, oil and gas while others defend their right to exploit these resources.
The negotiations fall in the midst of a conflict-driven energy crisis that has sharply spiked the cost of diesel, fertilisers and other essential commodities.
Guterres said it was “absurd” and “morally unacceptable” that nine fossil fuel majors would reap $95 billion in profits in a single quarter from the price hikes while ordinary people struggled to afford heating and fuel.

“We are talking about consolidated interests that are not easy to defeat,” Guterres told AFP at his final climate summit after a decade at the helm of the United Nations.
“Governments need to protect the interests of their peoples — not the interests of a group of companies,” he said of the oil and gas firms often in his crosshairs.
And that means no new fossil fuel projects, he said — even if industry groups apply concerted pressure on political leaders in an effort to protect their investments.
“Any new projects of fossil fuels do not make any sense,” said the 77-year-old former Portuguese prime minister, who steps down as secretary-general in December.

“Now, obviously, I would prefer that the countries that are in this COP, all would assume that position — including the organisers.”
Turkey celebrated the discovery of new oil fields on the opening day of COP31 while Australia, which is chairing the climate negotiations, faced criticism over recently approved coal mine expansions.
– Never surrender –
The wars in Ukraine and Iran, a pandemic, and paralysis in the Security Council have tested Guterres’ skills as a diplomat but on fossil fuels the UN chief has rarely pulled any punches.

From his global pulpit, he has railed against “the godfathers of climate chaos”, accusing the oil and gas lobby of “killing our planet” and governments of “subsidising suicide” by propping up the industry.

His fiery rhetoric has made him a champion among the climate movement — and something of a rarity at the COPs.
Neither Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese nor COP31 President Murat Kurum mentioned fossil fuels once by name during their keynote speeches to world leaders on Wednesday — despite being the main driver of climate change.
By contrast, Guterres received raucous ovations as he called for fossil fuels to “go the way of the dinosaurs” and castigated governments for stalling the transition to clean energy.
“This is an existential threat… we cannot minimise it. And I think we need to use a language that is clear enough for people to understand that we are really facing a severe risk at the present moment,” he said of his trademark flourishes.
“Secretary-General Guterres is a true global hero,” former US vice president Al Gore, himself a celebrated climate campaigner, told AFP in Antalya.
