The Nobel Peace Prize laureate said Guterres “deserves the thanks of the entire world and I hope the next secretary-general will follow his example”.
But for the thundering prose, Guterres leaves office with a world far hotter than when he took office in 2017 shortly after the landmark Paris Agreement took effect.
Despite the explosion of electric cars and solar power, fossil fuel demand is surging, global emissions are at record highs, and the 1.5C limit will be breached in a matter of years.
Most political leaders “have not yet fully understood that this is becoming a crisis moment” and without drastic cuts to planet-heating emissions, the world is condemned to a bleaker future, he said.
But “we have not lost the battle”, he said. “This is not the moment to surrender — this is the moment to fight back”.

sources.news_title: Amid energy crisis: Fossil fuel mega-profits 'morally unacceptable', Guterres tells AFP
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Thursday slammed soaring fossil fuel profits as "morally unacceptable" and demanded governments put their people ahead of the bottom lines of oil and gas giants.
In an exclusive interview with AFP at COP31, the outgoing UN chief said no country could pursue new fossil fuels while claiming to fight climate change -- including summit organisers Turkey and Australia.
The climate conference in Antalya has resurfaced old fault lines over fossil fuels, with some countries pushing for a faster exit from coal, oil and gas while others defend their right to exploit these resources.
The negotiations fall in the midst of a conflict-driven energy crisis that has sharply spiked the cost of diesel, fertilisers and other essential commodities.
Guterres said it was "absurd" and "morally unacceptable" that nine fossil fuel majors would reap $95 billion in profits in a single quarter from the price hikes while ordinary people struggled to afford heating and fuel.
"We are talking about consolidated interests that are not easy to defeat," Guterres told AFP at his final climate summit after a decade at the helm of the United Nations.
"Governments need to protect the interests of their peoples -- not the interests of a group of companies," he said of the oil and gas firms often in his crosshairs.
And that means no new fossil fuel projects, he said -- even if industry groups apply concerted pressure on political leaders in an effort to protect their investments.
"Any new projects of fossil fuels do not make any sense," said the 77-year-old former Portuguese prime minister, who steps down as secretary-general in December.
"Now, obviously, I would prefer that the countries that are in this COP, all would assume that position -- including the organisers."
Turkey celebrated the discovery of new oil fields on the opening day of COP31 while Australia, which is chairing the climate negotiations, faced criticism over recently approved coal mine expansions.
The wars in Ukraine and Iran, a pandemic, and paralysis in the Security Council have tested Guterres' skills as a diplomat but on fossil fuels the UN chief has rarely pulled any punches.
From his global pulpit, he has railed against "the godfathers of climate chaos", accusing the oil and gas lobby of "killing our planet" and governments of "subsidising suicide" by propping up the industry.
His fiery rhetoric has made him a champion among the climate movement -- and something of a rarity at the COPs.
Neither Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese nor COP31 President Murat Kurum mentioned fossil fuels once by name during their keynote speeches to world leaders on Wednesday -- despite being the main driver of climate change.
By contrast, Guterres received raucous ovations as he called for fossil fuels to "go the way of the dinosaurs" and castigated governments for stalling the transition to clean energy.
"This is an existential threat... we cannot minimise it. And I think we need to use a language that is clear enough for people to understand that we are really facing a severe risk at the present moment," he said of his trademark flourishes.
"Secretary-General Guterres is a true global hero," former US vice president Al Gore, himself a celebrated climate campaigner, told AFP in Antalya.
The Nobel Peace Prize laureate said Guterres "deserves the thanks of the entire world and I hope the next secretary-general will follow his example".
But for the thundering prose, Guterres leaves office with a world far hotter than when he took office in 2017 shortly after the landmark Paris Agreement took effect.
Despite the explosion of electric cars and solar power, fossil fuel demand is surging, global emissions are at record highs, and the 1.5C limit will be breached in a matter of years.
Most political leaders "have not yet fully understood that this is becoming a crisis moment" and without drastic cuts to planet-heating emissions, the world is condemned to a bleaker future, he said.
But "we have not lost the battle", he said. "This is not the moment to surrender -- this is the moment to fight back".

sources.news_title: UN chief calls for windfall taxes on 'unjustifiable' energy profits
sources.text:
Energy sector profits that swelled alongside global conflicts are "morally unjustifiable" and should face additional taxes to fund climate measures, according to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres.
"There's something fundamentally wrong," Guterres said Thursday in an interview with Bloomberg Television at the annual UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. "They are making these profits with an activity that is causing severe damage to the global environment and severe damage in the acceleration of climate change."
Guterres has held discussions with governments about an additional levy on oil and gas companies, and on Wednesday told global leaders at the COP31 talks that a group of nine major producers had reported collective profits of $95 billion in the last quarter — many multiples higher than funding available to respond to climate disasters.
"Those taxes should be used to alleviate the situation of those that are suffering," Guterres said in the interview. Nations have existing mechanisms "able to tax windfall profits – it's a political decision, it's not a technical problem," he said.
European fossil fuel producers faced additional levies after Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent fuel prices soaring, and tax collectors have been studying potential similar responses to the volatility triggered by the Iran war. The U.K. announced in May it would close a loophole that would prevent overseas oil and gas firms from paying little or no corporation tax in the country, while Poland's government has imposed a further tax on producers of liquid fuel.
The European Commission, the bloc's executive branch, is analyzing the potential impacts of imposing a tax on windfall energy profits. It would be a "good idea" to use any such levy to provide finance for climate adaptation measures, according to Teresa Ribera, the EU's anti-trust chief.
Global leaders and diplomats gathered at the COP31 summit in Turkey are aiming to reinvigorate efforts on reducing emissions, delivering climate finance and the transition away from fossil fuels, particularly after a series of deadly heat waves and wildfires this year. Greenhouse gas emissions caused by human activity have led the planet's temperature to rise 1.47C above the average of pre-industrial times for the first nine months of 2026, according to the UN's World Meteorological Organization.
Debate around taxing energy profits is gaining traction in some quarters as other sources of climate funding have dried up. "If this isn't the moment for governments to act, when will it be," said Fanny Petitbon, a policy analyst with environmental nonprofit 350.org.
The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, created to help developing nations cope with climate disasters, currently stands at only $600 million, according to Guterres. "This looks like a joke," he said.
Even so, many governments are reluctant to act on company profits."The power of the oil and gas lobby is very high," Guterres said. "Especially in some countries where they fund candidates for the sovereignty bodies of the country."
In addition to climate change, artificial intelligence is also a potential "existential threat" to humanity, and requires a "multilateral system of oversight of the safety risks," Guterres said.
"I believe it's in the interests of the companies to make sure that those risks are eliminated," he said. "It's also the guarantee of their own future, because if the companies lose control of their products, they will also not be able to make profits with those products."

sources.news_title: UN chief says climate summit must ‘tell the truth’ on warming, fossil fuels
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the high-level meeting of the climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Wednesday, calling for faster action to phase out fossil fuels.
“The most important thing we do is tell the truth about climate change,” Guterres said. “The last four years have been the warmest on the planet ever.”
To save the planet, he said, the pace of the transition away from fossil fuels must accelerate. Coal must be phased out within 15 years, and the use of oil and gas must be cut by a third, he said.
“We must contribute so that poor countries can also reach the goal of replacing fossil energy with renewable energy, before it is too late,” he said.
Guterres said those who profit most from fossil energy should contribute the most. He pointed to the enormous profits of oil companies and compared them with what he called “the relatively modest sum” given to the fund for loss and damage for vulnerable countries.
“It is time for governments to tax these companies and use the money to help vulnerable countries get back on their feet,” he said.
“The polluter must pay,” Guterres concluded.

The world is heading for an “irrecoverable overshoot” of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts, according to new analysis. Governments have stalled for so long on cutting planet-heating emissions that the damage may no longer be reversible, the report warns.

sources.news_title: COP31 Greens MEPs Warn of Climate Summit Failure
sources.text:
Greens MEPs say they are pessimistic about the prospects of the latest global climate event yielding any firm results.
Michael Bloss and were speaking in Brussels as world leaders and negotiators gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31.
Both agree that Antalya will be a crucial moment for the world to move forward on the phase-out of fossil fuels, at a time when record heatwaves, floods and wildfires show the climate crisis is already here.
The EU’s role will be essential in securing global momentum in the fight against climate change, they say.
But, speaking to this website before leaving for the talks, Bloss said he had little hope that 2 of the 3 things he hoped the conference might produce will actually happen.
The two are, he said, a greater commitment to phasing out fossil fuels and, secondly, encouraging the EU to come up with more financing for tackling climate change.
Bloss, who will be attending his 8th COP conference, said, “I expect nothing I have to say on these two things, especially without the US at the table”
The only positive outcome he foresees, he said, is on renewable-based electrification.
He is critical of the role of the EU on climate issues, saying it is guilty of providing “too little leadership.”
“The idea of a rules based order is being challenged like never before and the EU is right, of course, in defending it (rules based).But climate issues are central to this and the EU needs to provide more leadership in slowing the climate crisis. At present, I do not see that happening,” he said.
He pointed out that this was all the more necessary as Europe, in recent years, had been the “one continent in the world” that is experiencing climate change at its most acute.
Despite reservations in some quarters, he still believes the COP events have a role to play.
He said, “Yes, there are things may be more fit for purpose but, even so, I still think we would be worse off without it (COP).”
His comments are partly echoed by his group colleague Kai Tegethoff, also a German MEP, who will also attend the talks and told this site he expects COP31 to focus on electrification, saying, “I do understand the reasons for that.”
But he also hopes the conference will “still talk about” other issues, particularly phasing out fossil fuels and climate adaptation.
He too looks to the EU for more of a leadership role in the talks, saying, “It has lost this a bit but its role is to be demanding on the global stage. The question is: Is is ready to act?”
He is particularly scathing of the principle of unanimity at the COP talks.
At the event the long-standing rule of unanimity (consensus) is facing severe scrutiny and active circumvention by frustrated nations.
Under the standard United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) rules, formal decisions require consensus among all 198 parties, meaning a single objecting country can stall or veto global progress.
The MEP says that while this needs reforming he still believes the COP conference is a “valuable” chance for all parties to “come together and to see where we land.”
Speaking separately, Ciarán Cuffe, Co-Chair of the European Green Party, said, “With the US federal government once again absent from the climate negotiations, Europe must lead the global transition.”
Vula Tsetsi, Co-Chair of the European Green Party, said, “The EU cannot claim to be a global leader on climate change while weakening the European Green Deal and rolling back its own commitments. Europe must lead by example, ending public subsidies for fossil fuels and building a coalition for a fossil-free future.”

sources.news_title: Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate? - Times Kuwait
sources.text:
Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?
World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.
With extreme weather intensifying, climate finance declining and global temperatures nearing dangerous levels, UN chief Antonio Guterres urges world leaders to turn climate promises into urgent, practical action.
The discussions at COP31 highlight a widening gap between climate commitments and actual implementation.
The world is falling behind in the fight against climate change, with rising temperatures, extreme weather events and declining climate finance threatening to undermine international efforts to prevent catastrophic global warming, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye.
“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us,” Guterres told world leaders gathered for the UN climate summit, stressing that the slow international response has put the world on a dangerous path. However, he said countries still had the power to ensure that the temporary breach of the agreed temperature limit does not become permanent.
A United Nations report published last month warned that the world is set to exceed the temperature threshold countries committed to pursuing under the Paris Agreement. The warning comes amid a year marked by devastating climate-related disasters, including extreme heatwaves, worsening droughts and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered flooding, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing.
The impact of rising temperatures is also becoming increasingly visible across Europe, where rivers and lakes have been drying up amid prolonged heat and drought. These developments underline the growing urgency of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and strengthening the resilience of communities exposed to extreme weather.
With representatives from nearly 200 countries attending COP31, discussions are focusing on turning climate commitments into practical action, particularly by expanding electrification, accelerating clean energy investment and reducing dependence on fossil fuels.
However, the absence of the United States, the world’s largest historical emitter of greenhouse gases, has raised further concerns about international cooperation. Washington is not attending for the second consecutive year following President Donald Trump’s decision to withdraw the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025. Several other major economies, including Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, have also not sent their top leaders.
Climate finance remains one of the biggest obstacles to progress, with developing countries demanding greater financial support from wealthier nations to address a crisis to which they have contributed relatively little but whose consequences they often face most severely.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called on developed countries to take greater responsibility for climate financing, saying previous commitments and proposals had not been adequately translated into action. He said the objective of COP31 was to make it an implementation-focused summit.
The funding challenge has become more pressing following a decline in international financial commitments. A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public climate funding pledged under the Paris Agreement for developing countries fell by more than 70 percent in 2026. Several multi-year funding commitments expired in 2025, while the United States stepped back from international climate efforts and some European countries reduced aid budgets.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union remained committed to supporting developing countries, noting that Europe contributed more than 32 billion euros last year towards climate action. She stressed that moving away from fossil fuels was in the common interest, pointing to the growing economic, environmental and energy-security costs of maintaining the existing energy system.
The vulnerability of developing countries was highlighted by Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine, who warned that every fraction of a degree of additional warming would bring greater destruction, loss and financial pressure.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the current period as a critical decade for climate action and called for stronger international cooperation to unlock investment in clean energy technologies, accelerate electrification and increase protection for the world’s oceans.
A key proposal at COP31 is the 35-by-35 electrification pledge, which aims to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035. Supporters argue that electrification, backed by renewable energy, can reduce emissions while improving energy security and limiting exposure to fossil fuel price fluctuations.
Guterres noted that three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, leaving them vulnerable to price shocks beyond their control. He said the transition to renewable energy could help address both energy insecurity and the cost-of-living crisis.
The conference has also brought attention to the environmental consequences of armed conflicts. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called for compensation for environmental damage allegedly caused by US and Israeli strikes since February, including oil leaks linked to attacks on tankers.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva warned that international attention had shifted away from climate action towards wars and trade disputes, weakening the momentum built at previous climate conferences. He urged governments to maintain cooperation and reaffirmed Brazil’s commitment to protecting the Amazon rainforest, which plays a critical role in regulating the global climate.
The discussions at COP31 highlight a widening gap between climate commitments and actual implementation. With temperatures continuing to rise, extreme weather becoming more damaging and financial support remaining uncertain, the summit faces the challenge of turning political promises into measurable action before the consequences of global warming become increasingly difficult to reverse.

This article is published in association with United Nations.
UN chief António Guterres called for a new global climate justice agreement at COP31 on Wednesday, urging governments to tax fossil fuel companies to help countries bearing the brunt of a crisis they did little to cause. His appeal came as world leaders gathered in Antalya amid unresolved questions over climate finance and the future of fossil fuels.
Today at COP31
- Leaders’ Summit: Guterres calls for climate justice and taxes on oil giants.
- Negotiations: Disagreements persist over adaptation finance.
- Zero Waste Day: Methane and innovative solutions headline the discussions.
Today saw packed corridors at the COP31 conference venue in Antalya as world leaders arrived for a two-day high-level Summit, bringing tighter security, road closures and an early start for delegates, some of whom reached the venue as early as 5 a.m.
Those who arrived before dawn were rewarded with a spectacular sunrise. Later, at the opening ceremony, traditional Turkish dancing, colourful performances, videos and even a COP31 theme song gave the opening ceremony an unusually festive air for a gathering confronting one of the world’s most pressing crises.
But the day’s most memorable message came from the Secretary-General, who accused polluters of delaying action, and once again warned that the climate crisis is advancing faster than global efforts to contain it.
“Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time,” he said, reminding world leaders that even if current national plans are fully implemented, the planet is heading towards more than 2.5°C of warming by century’s end.
But he insisted that breaching the 1.5°C threshold does not mean giving up. “Science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder” the UN chief said, stressing that every fraction of a degree of warming avoided matters.
Soundcloud
A new deal for climate justice
Against that backdrop, the Secretary-General proposed a ‘climate justice compact’ to help developing countries move away from fossil fuels while protecting those already suffering from climate change.
“We cannot demand that countries transform their economies while denying them the means to do so,” he said.
The proposed compact rests on four priorities:
Tweet URL
- Accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels through national plans that protect workers and communities, while expanding renewable energy.
- Protect vulnerable populations with early-warning systems, stronger adaptation measures and faster support after climate disasters.
- Deliver affordable climate finance, with wealthy countries fulfilling their commitments and more investment reaching developing nations.
- Strengthen international cooperation to overcome trade barriers, technological divides and geopolitical rivalries.
Polluters must pay
The UN chief took aim at fossil fuel interests, accusing them of distorting science and delaying climate action.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he declared. “The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”
He contrasted the $95 billion earned by the world’s nine largest oil companies in one quarter with the roughly $600 million received by the international fund helping vulnerable countries recover from climate-related loss and damage.
That was equivalent to just 14 hours of those companies’ profits, he said, urging governments to tax windfall profits.
“Polluters must pay”, a line that earned him an ovation in the plenary.
Leaders confront unfinished business
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, whose country is co-hosting COP31 in Antalya with Australia, acknowledged that three decades of climate negotiations had failed to deliver sufficient results.
“This success at the level of ideas has not produced the same results when it comes to implementation,” he said, calling for greater support for developing countries.
Brazilian President Lula da Silva, meanwhile, warned that climate change was losing ground on the international agenda as wars and trade disputes overshadowed the fight against global warming.
“We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations,” he said, defending international cooperation at a time when climate science and multilateralism are increasingly under attack.
Mr. Lula also announced that Brazil would develop national roadmaps to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels and end deforestation, building on the work of last year’s COP30, which was held in the Amazon.
Tackling methane: The ‘climate emergency brake’
An invisible gas that traps more than 80 times as much heat as carbon dioxide over 20 years featured prominently during Wednesday’s “Zero Waste” thematic day.
Methane, released by fossil fuel operations, agriculture and rotting waste, is responsible for nearly a third of global warming to date. At a special event, Mr. Guterres called on the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) to develop a global standard for near-zero methane emissions from oil and gas.
UNEP is already tracking major leaks from space, using satellites and artificial intelligence to identify emissions and alert governments and companies.
Julia Ferini, who leads UNEP’s International Methane Emissions Observatory, told UN News that the system has helped reduce emissions in 45 cases across 13 countries.
She pointed to a recent case in Iraq, where a damaged gas pipeline had been leaking methane for two years, producing emissions equivalent to those of 350,000 cars. The leak was stopped by applying a coating to the corroded pipe.
“Methane is our climate emergency brake,” she said, explaining that cutting this short-lived gas could slow warming relatively quickly, buying time to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.
Yet despite more than 5,000 alerts issued since 2023, barely one in eight has received a response, the UN chief noted.
Worms turning waste into something useful
And while negotiators in Antalya wrestle with how to accelerate climate action, young entrepreneurs are already putting some of them into practice.
In Botswana, Makwena Moesi is tackling food waste with an unusual workforce: more than half a million worms.
Her company, Viva Organica, collects organic waste from food retailers and turns it into fertilizer through a process known as vermicomposting, improving soil health while keeping waste out of landfills.
The business has already processed more than 1,000 tonnes of organic waste.
But Ms. Moesi, a biologist by training, says climate-friendly solutions must also make economic sense.
“A farmer does not wake up in the morning thinking about what am I gonna do to help sequester this amount of carbon dioxide from the air,” she told UN News.
Instead, she said, farmers want to know how much food they can grow, how to improve their harvests and whether they can afford the products that could help them.
Where negotiations stand
Alongside the leaders’ speeches, negotiators continued grappling with key unresolved issues:
- Climate finance: Developing countries pushed for more predictable funding, warning of shortfalls in support for adaptation and climate action.
- Loss and damage: Nepal’s request for assistance following a glacial collapse raised questions about how quickly emergency funding can reach affected countries.
- Emissions cuts: Countries disagreed over how long the UN’s programme to accelerate emissions reductions should continue and how it should operate.
- A just transition: Negotiators discussed a new mechanism to help countries shift to cleaner economies while protecting workers and communities.

sources.news_title: Report warns world faces ‘irrecoverable overshoot’ on warming without rapid action – Axadle
sources.text:
The world is on course for an “irrecoverable overshoot” of dangerous warming unless governments turn away from fossil fuels and accelerate emissions cuts, a new report warns.
The latest assessment from the Climate Action Tracker (CAT) initiative was released as countries gathered in Turkey for COP31, the United Nations climate talks. It says global efforts to tackle climate change have stalled for a fifth straight year.
There are signs of momentum in some areas. Clean electricity supplied all additional global power demand in 2025, while China and India expanded renewable energy at record speed. Electric vehicle sales also reached new highs, and deforestation in the Amazon dropped sharply.
Yet the report says the shift away from fossil fuels – the main source of greenhouse gas emissions when burned for transport, heating, electricity and industry – remains far too slow.
Based on the climate policies and clean-energy measures governments have adopted so far, the world is headed for 2.7C of warming by 2100. That is slightly higher than the 2.6C forecast issued last year and matches projections made from 2021 to 2024.
Even if governments fulfilled their 2030 and 2035 emissions-cutting targets under the Paris Agreement – the international treaty designed to limit warming to 1.5C and avoid the most dangerous effects of climate change – warming would still reach 2.6C, unchanged from last year.
In the most optimistic scenario, with countries delivering every pledge and target aimed at reaching net zero emissions, global temperatures would rise by 1.9C by the end of the century.
The 1.5C Paris target is expected to be breached within the next few years. Experts say governments must still act to reduce both the scale and length of that overshoot, with the aim of bringing temperatures back below 1.5C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
A sharp fall in Amazon deforestation is among the report’s positive findings
Bill Hare, chief executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics, said governments faced a stark choice between continuing to back fossil fuels and embracing increasingly affordable alternatives.
“The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases, and disasters that they are unable to adapt to, or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever,” he said.
“The imminence of breaching 1.5C cannot be an excuse to open the door to defeatism – the focus has to be on accelerating action to limit the magnitude and duration of overshoot.
“Every increment of warming above 1.5C means even more significant consequences across climate, nature and human systems.”
Scientists say a breach of 1.5C would intensify extreme weather, including deadly heatwaves, floods, storms and droughts. It would also drive sea-level rise and increase the risk of catastrophic, irreversible damage to natural systems such as coral reefs and rainforests.
An analysis released earlier this week by the Global Carbon Budget initiative pointed to a modest 0.4% fall in fossil-fuel carbon emissions this year, attributed to the rapid expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict.
Dr Niklas Hohne, of CAT partner organisation NewClimate Institute, said the disruption surrounding the Strait of Hormuz had highlighted the risks of relying on fossil fuels in an unstable geopolitical environment.
“With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz exposing our vulnerability to geopolitical shocks, the case for renewables and electrification has never been stronger,” he said.
“It does appear that global emissions could be on the verge of a peak and a much faster decline than we had previously thought.”
Latest Climate Change stories
But Sarah Heck, a policy analyst at Climate Analytics and the report’s lead author, said governments were “simply not moving fast enough to adopt the policies that would enable us to escape from the emerging overshoot trap”.
“Worse, several are taking their foot off the accelerator and slowing their climate action – or in cases such as the USA, Canada and New Zealand – rolling it back at a staggering level,” she added.
As a result, CAT said long-term warming is expected to pass the 1.5C threshold at around 2030.
To keep any overshoot of 1.5C as limited as possible, emissions cuts would need to accelerate from roughly 4% a year through 2030 to 7% annually during the first half of the 2030s, followed by reductions of 9% a year between 2035 and 2050.
That would exceed the 7% fall in fossil-fuel carbon emissions recorded in 2020, when Covid-19 lockdowns brought economic activity around the world to a halt.

sources.news_title: UN Global Compact Calls for Faster Climate Action as Business Leaders Gather at COP31
sources.text:
ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Business and UN leaders gathered at COP31 today to address one of the most pressing challenges in global climate action: how to turn corporate commitments into measurable emissions reductions at a time of growing political uncertainty and economic pressure.
Convened by the United Nations Global Compact, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and UN Climate Change, the 14th Annual High-Level Meeting of Caring for Climate brought together chief executives and senior representatives from business, finance, Government, civil society and the United Nations to identify practical ways to accelerate climate action and overcome barriers that individual companies cannot tackle alone.
The meeting came amid renewed warnings from UNEP that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C of warming within the next few years. With the window for limiting the scale and duration of that overshoot narrowing, participants examined how businesses can sustain science-based climate ambition while translating transition plans into tangible results.
“We meet at a defining moment for climate action. The magnitude and duration of the overshoot depends on the choices we make today, and returning to 1.5 degrees remains possible but only through urgent and sustained emissions reductions,” said Sanda Ojiambo, UN Assistant Secretary-General, CEO and Executive Director of the UN Global Compact. “The next chapter of climate leadership will be defined not by the commitments we make but by the problems we solve, the emissions we cut and the clean, green energy transition that we deliver.”
Ms. Ojiambo stressed that many of the policies, technologies and solutions needed to accelerate climate action already exist. The challenge is deploying them at the speed and scale required. While corporate climate commitments have grown, implementation continues to lag, held back by policy uncertainty, inadequate infrastructure, financing constraints and continued fossil fuel subsidies.
Building on the UN Secretary-General’s engagement with business leaders at September’s UN Private Sector Forum, where companies signalled their willingness to invest in the clean energy transition, the meeting focused on the conditions needed to turn that ambition into action across the wider economy.
Discussions centred on three priorities: strengthening the credibility of corporate climate action, improving accountability for results and accelerating collective action to address systemic barriers.
Participants examined how science-based targets and credible transition plans must be embedded in business strategy, operations and investment decisions, rather than treated as standalone sustainability commitments. They also explored the importance of transparent reporting, reliable data and measurable emissions reductions in demonstrating progress, identifying gaps and building confidence among investors, policymakers and other stakeholders.
A central theme was that corporate ambition alone cannot deliver the transition. Clear and predictable government policies, investment in infrastructure and greater access to finance are essential to enable businesses to move faster, particularly in emerging and developing economies. Participants also considered how stronger collaboration between business, Governments, financial institutions and the United Nations can help overcome these obstacles.
The meeting also considered how corporate climate leadership must extend beyond individual companies, including through responsible policy engagement, collaboration across value chains and support for the wider economic changes needed to achieve a just and resilient transition.
Launched in 2007, Caring for Climate is a longstanding partnership between the UN Global Compact, UNEP and UN Climate Change to advance business leadership on climate action and strengthen dialogue between the private sector and policymakers.
The High-Level Meeting is a centrepiece of the UN Global Compact’s wider programme at COP31, which includes more than 20 sessions organized with its Country Networks on the clean energy transition, industrial decarbonization, circularity, climate resilience and a just transition.
About Caring for Climate

sources.news_title: Polluters must pay, says the UN chief at COP31
UN Chief demands fossil fuel taxes at COP31 Summit in Antalya
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres demanded a new global climate justice agreement at COP31 on Wednesday. He urged governments to tax fossil fuel firms to fund vulnerable nations.
World leaders packed the Antalya conference venue for the two-day summit. Organizers enforced tight security and road closures as delegates arrived before dawn.
Traditional Turkish dances and a theme song gave the opening ceremony a festive mood. However, Guterres quickly shifted the focus to the escalating climate emergency.
A New Compact for Climate Justice
Guterres warned that current national plans push the planet toward 2.5°C of warming. He urged leaders to fight harder rather than surrender to rising temperatures.
The UN chief proposed a climate justice compact resting on four priorities. Countries must accelerate renewable transitions, protect vulnerable populations, deliver affordable finance, and strengthen global cooperation.
“We cannot demand that countries transform their economies while denying them the means to do so,” Guterres told delegates.
Making Polluters Pay
Guterres accused fossil fuel lobbyists of distorting science and delaying action. He contrasted $95 billion in quarterly oil profits against $600 million in international recovery funds.
“Polluters must pay,” Guterres declared, earning a loud ovation from the plenary hall. He urged governments to tax windfall fossil fuel profits immediately.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan noted that past negotiations failed to deliver real implementation. Brazilian President Lula da Silva warned that wars and tariffs now overshadow climate survival.
Pulling the Methane Emergency Brake
During Wednesday’s Zero Waste day, leaders targeted methane emissions. This potent gas traps 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide over two decades.
Guterres asked the UN Environment Programme to set near-zero methane standards for oil and gas. Currently, satellites track leaks globally, yet companies ignore most UN alerts.
Grassroots Innovation and Deadlocked Talks
Meanwhile, young entrepreneurs demonstrated practical climate solutions. In Botswana, biologist Makwena Moesi uses half a million worms to convert 1,000 tonnes of food waste into affordable fertilizer.
Inside the negotiating rooms, delegates clashed over unresolved issues. Developing nations demanded predictable climate finance, faster disaster relief for crises like Nepal’s glacial collapse, and clearer emission timelines.

sources.news_title: Report Warns World Near Irreversible Climate Warming Overshoot - Jowhar News Leader
sources.text:
Report Warns World Near Irreversible Climate Warming Overshoot
The world is speeding toward an “irrecoverable overshoot” of dangerous warming unless governments turn away from fossil fuels and deliver rapid emissions cuts, a new report has cautioned.
The latest assessment from the Climate Action Tracker (CAT) initiative, published as nations gather for COP31, the United Nations climate talks in Turkey, says momentum on climate action has flatlined for a fifth straight year.
The report points to several bright spots: clean electricity is set to cover all additional global power demand in 2025; China and India are rolling out renewables at record speed; electric vehicle deployment has reached new highs; and deforestation in the Amazon has fallen sharply.
Even with those gains, CAT warns that the shift away from fossil fuels is not happening quickly enough. Coal, oil and gas remain the dominant sources of the greenhouse gas emissions that heat the planet when burned for transport, heating, electricity and industry.
Rising energy demand, combined with new fossil fuel infrastructure still being built, is keeping global emissions on an upward trajectory, the report says.
Based on the climate and clean-energy policies governments currently have in place, CAT finds the world is now headed for 2.7C of warming by 2100. That is slightly higher than the 2.6C estimate in last year’s update, and matches the projections made from 2021 to 2024.
Even if countries fully achieved their 2030 and 2035 emissions-cutting targets under the Paris Agreement — the global pact designed to limit warming to 1.5C and avoid the most dangerous impacts of climate change — warming would still reach 2.6C, unchanged from last year, according to CAT.
In a more optimistic case in which nations deliver on every pledge and long-term target to bring emissions down to net zero overall, CAT says temperatures would rise by 1.9C by the end of the century.
Researchers also stress the Paris benchmark of 1.5C is likely to be breached within the next few years, making it crucial to curb both the scale and the duration of the overshoot — and to reduce temperatures to below 1.5C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
A fall sharp in deforestation in the Amazon is a positive, the report says
Bill Hare, chief executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics, said: “The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases, and disasters that they are unable to adapt to, or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever.
“The imminence of breaching 1.5C cannot be an excuse to open the door to defeatism – the focus has to be on accelerating action to limit the magnitude and duration of overshoot.
“Every increment of warming above 1.5C means even more significant consequences across climate, nature and human systems.”
Scientists say crossing 1.5C of global warming would intensify extreme weather, including deadly heatwaves, floods, storms and drought. It would also accelerate sea-level rise and increase the risk of catastrophic and irreversible damage to natural systems such as coral reefs and rainforests.
Separate analysis released earlier this week by the Global Carbon Budget initiative indicated a modest 0.4% decline in carbon emissions from fossil fuels this year, attributing the drop to expanding solar and wind capacity and the Iran conflict.
Dr Niklas Hohne of CAT partner organisation NewClimate Institute said: “With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz exposing our vulnerability to geopolitical shocks, the case for renewables and electrification has never been stronger.
“It does appear that global emissions could be on the verge of a peak and a much faster decline than we had previously thought.”
Latest climate change stories
Still, Sarah Heck, a policy analyst at Climate Analytics and lead author of the report, said the overall pace of change remains dangerously slow.
Governments are “simply not moving fast enough to adopt the policies that would enable us to escape from the emerging overshoot trap,” she said.
“Worse, several are taking their foot off the accelerator and slowing their climate action – or in cases such as the USA, Canada and New Zealand – rolling it back at a staggering level,” she added.
As a result, CAT expects long-term warming to push beyond the 1.5C limit around 2030.
To keep the overshoot as small as possible, the report says emissions cuts must accelerate sharply — from about 4% a year through 2030 to 7% a year in the first half of the 2030s, then to 9% a year from 2035 to 2050.
For comparison, carbon emissions from fossil fuels fell 7% in 2020, driven by Covid-19 lockdowns worldwide.

sources.news_title: PM Mottley calls for global action on climate and debt crisis at COP31
sources.text:
In an address consistent with her firm approach to tackling climate change and mitigating climate risks, Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley told world leaders at COP31 in Türkiye that a global movement is needed to address the issue.
Recalling her appeal to world leaders at COP26 in Glasgow five years ago to make greater efforts to achieve the 1.5-degree Celsius target, which she said was critical for survival, Ms Mottley noted that the evidence was now clear: the world had not tried hard enough.
Referring to climate-related disasters that have devastated livelihoods and economies across the world, the Prime Minister stressed that “the climate does not negotiate with geopolitics”.
She maintained that a fund without financial resources “is a monument, not a mechanism”, while calling on world leaders to break the cycle of debt crises.
Ms Mottley also recommended an investor-led approach, which she said could provide a “win-win” solution.

sources.news_title: Guterres Targets Fossil Fuel Lobby As Leaders At COP31 Divide Over Debt, Finance And War
sources.text:
ANTALYA – In his last climate summit address as UN secretary-general, António Guterres accused fossil fuel interests of “making a killing while killing our planet”, and warned that a world set to blow past 1.5°C of warming was on a “path to mutually assured destruction.”
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” Guterres told the leaders. “But that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. But fossil fuels do.”
The nine largest oil companies made $95 billion in profit last quarter alone, he noted, while the fund launched at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to pay for losses from climate disasters has received around $600 million, roughly what those companies earn in 14 hours.
“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us,” Guterres said. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”
Speaking as more than 70 world leaders gathered in Antalya for two days of speeches, Guterres appealed for unity at a time of deep divisions over war, debt and who should pay for the costs of a warming planet.
“We do not need countries to agree on everything,” Guterres said. “But we do need to cooperate on the things no country can solve alone, and the climate process itself must evolve. Negotiations matter, but success must be measured on the ground.”
Leaders of the three biggest emitters stay home
The leaders’ summit marks the point where COP31 turns from procedural wrangling to politics, before the talks close on 20 November. After a year dominated by war, inflation and an oil price shock, the path to a true breakthrough in Antalya looks steep.
“Chaos in global energy markets and climate disasters are supercharging inflation,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell told leaders. “The political costs of fossil fuel dependency are unforgiving.”
A procession of heads of state, from Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, accepted that warming can no longer be held below the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C limit, the north star of COP negotiations for the past decade.
Despite the accelerating crisis, heads of state from many of the world’s largest economies – and the three top emitters in China, India and the US – are skipping the summit.
Leaders who stayed home included China’s Xi Jinping and India’s Narendra Modi, as well as France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz. The United States, the second-largest emitter, sent no official delegation for the second year running.
“It is a disgrace that only one G7 head of state and a handful of G20 leaders are attending the summit,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa. “The world’s biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others.”
A White House official told Spectrum News the summit “rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world.”
“This concern turned into silence,” Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said of climate’s place at G7 and G20 summits. “We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations.”
‘Fight harder’
“Science tells us an overshoot above [1.5°C] is now inevitable,” Guterres said. “But science is not telling us to surrender. It’s telling us to fight harder. The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be.”
The World Meteorological Organization put the global average temperature from January to September at 1.47°C above pre-industrial levels in its latest update. An El Niño forecast to reach record strength by December will push that higher, giving a “new meaning to the phrase off the charts,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said on Monday.
Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands, whose atolls average about two metres above sea level, told leaders the global response to overshoot must be “overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”
“Overshoot means waves eating away our shores, flooding that destroys towns, schools, hospitals,” she said. “In July, I went to my home island. I saw coral, bright and lush beneath the water, as it has been throughout my life. I returned just a few months later, to find half [of it] white from bleaching.”
Most countries want the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN body that assesses climate science, to finish its next reports in time for the 2028 global review of climate progress, known as the global stocktake. Oil exporters Saudi Arabia and Russia have pushed back, along with India.
“We have seen efforts to undermine the IPCC and to [block] its reports informing the next global stocktake,” Heine said. “Our Pacific scientists tell us the work can and should be completed on time.”
Trillion-dollar hurdle
“Developing countries pay nearly $1 trillion in interest on public debt,” said Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, whose country hosts COP32 next year. “[Early action] should begin here, with every pledge of finance answering three questions: how much, by when, on what terms.”
The UN trade and development agency, UNCTAD, puts the 2025 bill for developing nation interest payments at $995 billion and counts 3.7 billion people living in countries that spend more on interest than on either health or education.
Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations, told leaders that just 0.2% of climate finance goes to small island developing states to help them adapt to climate change. “This must change,” he said.
“We cannot demand that countries transform their economies while denying them the means to do so,” Guterres said. “Emerging and developing economies outside China are home to nearly two-thirds of humanity, yet they receive less than one-fifth of global clean-energy investment.”
Stiell said the talks would focus on “delivering, and improving access to finance – without reopening previous agreements,” leaving untouched the Baku target. Developing countries went into the 2024 talks in Baku seeking $1.3 trillion a year and left with a pledge under which developed countries agreed to mobilise $300 billion a year by 2035. The latest OECD figures show they provided and mobilised $136.7 billion in 2024, less than half that sum.
On opening day, developing countries won a dedicated agenda item on whether rich nations are meeting their legal duty to provide finance, over EU objections.
The dinosaur lobby is in the room
“Their strategy is simple,” Guterres said of the fossil fuel lobby. “Distort the science. Delay the policy. Delay the action. Delay the accountability.”
On Monday, the day COP31 opened, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced that Türkiye’s Gabar region now produces about 84,000 barrels of oil a day from 184 wells, and unveiled two new fields. Türkiye’s emissions rose by 24.4 million tonnes in 2025, the second-largest increase of any country after the United States, UNEP reported last month.
“Every new oil well drilled, every piece of coal extracted, is a threat to my country’s future,” Heine said. “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate, but something to fear.”
The presidency’s flagship pledge, to raise electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, does not require that extra power to come from clean sources. “Electrification is important,” Heine added, “but must be linked to renewable generation.”
In a fiery address in which the Turkish president declared that “unnecessarily cutting down a healthy tree is, in fact, equal to killing a person”, Erdoğan told leaders that developed countries “that have historically consumed the global carbon budget should assume greater responsibility for emissions reductions and financing,” reopening one of the oldest fault lines in climate talks: who counts as a donor.
No new donors
The 1992 UN climate convention puts the duty to provide climate finance on a list of wealthy nations known as Annex II: the United States, Japan, Germany and 20 other countries that belonged to the OECD in 1992, plus the European Union.
Russia, China and the Gulf states were never on the Annex II list. Despite decades of growth that have made China the world’s second-largest economy and Qatar and the United Arab Emirates among the richest countries per person, they insist they are not donors and will not become ones.
The Paris Agreement only encourages other countries to contribute voluntarily, which some do on their own terms: China says it has provided and mobilized more than 177 billion yuan, about $24.5 billion, for other developing countries since 2016, and the UAE launched a $30 billion climate investment fund when it hosted the 2023 summit in Dubai.
In an interview with Russian state media Interfax before the summit, Russia’s top climate envoy drew a red line reflecting non-donor states’ attitude.
“There are issues, if not ‘red lines,’ that we do not support,” Ruslan Edelgeriev, President Vladimir Putin’s special representative for climate, said. “The first is the rapid abandonment of hydrocarbons. The second issue is that they are trying to force Russia to become a ‘donor’ … we are not donors; this is purely voluntary.”
At Russia’s pavilion, an exhibit on its fleet of nuclear-powered icebreakers showcases how the country stands to profit from a warming planet, as melting sea ice opens the Northern Sea Route, an Arctic shortcut to Asia.
Russia’s long-term climate strategy, filed with the UN, says climate change “creates new opportunities” for the country’s trade and economy, including “an increase in the navigation period” on the route.

sources.news_title: Fund life, not war, leaders tell UN climate summit
sources.text:
- Leaders urge redirecting soaring defense budgets to climate action, find money for life, not death.
- Wars and rearmament are degrading land, water and air, threatening vulnerable nations' survival and accelerating environmental harm.
- Climate has been sidelined as arms and tariffs dominate the global agenda; leaders call restoring funding priorities for future generations.
With conflicts and defence spending surging worldwide, several leaders and environmental groups on Wednesday urged heads of state at the UN climate summit to redirect funds from wars to saving the planet.
“We are told there is no money, but the spending on war grows,” said Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine, whose country is among the most vulnerable to rising sea levels.
“The greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: find money for life, not death,” she told the COP31 conference in Turkey.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has presided over a sharp drop in deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, said climate change had “disappeared” from the global agenda.
“We’ve turned to talking more about arms and tariffs than the survival of future generations,” he said.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan echoed the warning.
“Nature — no less than people — is also paying a heavy price for armed conflicts. The starkest example of this is Gaza,” he told the summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.
With wars in Ukraine, the Middle East and elsewhere and geopolitical volatility spurring widespread rearmament, global defence spending hit nearly $3 trillion in 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga summed up the environmental impact of his country’s war, from “poisoned soil” to deforestation and birds building nests from drones’ fibre-optic cables.
“For most countries here, the energy transition is a matter of policy. For Ukraine it’s a matter of survival,” he said.
“Russia is at war with our people and with our land, our water, our air.”
Climate campaigner Tasneem Essop said discussion of soaring defence spending was lacking at the annual talks.
“Rich nations come here to say, we don’t have public finance. And yet they have the public finance to spend so much on wars,” Essop, head of the Climate Action Network, told AFP.
Host country Turkey plans to increase military spending by 229 percent in 2027, as it and fellow NATO members bolster their defence budgets.
Turkey’s COP31 president, Murat Kurum, had nevertheless said in September: “Every cent allocated to defence should also be allocated to preserving life on this planet.”

sources.news_title: Guterres warns climate crisis outrunning world, calls for urgent fossil fuel transition - EnviroNews - latest environment news, climate change, renewable energy
sources.text:
United Nations Secretary-General, António Guterres, has warned that the climate crisis is advancing faster than global efforts to contain it, urging world leaders to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels, scale up climate finance and strengthen support for vulnerable countries.
Guterres gave the warning on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, while addressing the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya, Türkiye, where he called for urgent and coordinated action to prevent the consequences of global warming from becoming increasingly devastating.
He said global greenhouse gas emissions reached record levels in 2025, while the last four years were the hottest ever recorded, with climate-related disasters increasingly threatening lives, livelihoods and economies worldwide.
“Our first climate duty is to tell the truth. The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us,” Guterres said.
He also criticised the continued influence of fossil fuel interests, accusing the industry of profiting from activities that contribute to the destruction of the planet.
Reflecting on the 2015 Paris Agreement, which established the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, the UN chief acknowledged that a temporary overshoot of the threshold had become inevitable.
However, he insisted that this should not be interpreted as a reason to abandon climate action, stressing that governments still have the power to determine the extent, duration and consequences of the overshoot.
“Science tells us an overshoot above that level is now inevitable. But science is not telling us to surrender. It’s telling us to fight harder,” he said.
Guterres outlined three major lessons from the past decade, which he said should guide global climate action over the next ten years.
The first, according to him, is that exponential change is possible, citing the rapid growth of renewable energy and electric vehicles as evidence that technological transformation can happen within a relatively short period.
He noted that solar power, which accounted for just one per cent of global electricity generation a decade ago, met nearly three-quarters of the growth in global electricity demand last year.
Similarly, electric vehicles, which represented approximately one per cent of new car sales ten years ago, are expected to account for nearly one-third of sales this year.
He added that clean energy had become the cheapest source of new electricity across most parts of the world, demonstrating that the transition was economically viable.
His second lesson was that the economic and energy security arguments for continued dependence on fossil fuels were weakening.
According to Guterres, three-quarters of the world’s population live in countries that import fossil fuels, leaving them vulnerable to international price shocks and geopolitical conflicts.
He called for a just, orderly and equitable transition to renewable energy, while warning that powerful fossil fuel interests continued to obstruct progress through misinformation, policy delays and resistance to accountability.
“The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. But fossil fuels do,” he said, calling on governments to end their dependence on fossil fuels.
On the third lesson, Guterres said global climate action remained far below the pace required to meet the Paris Agreement goals.
He explained that global emissions needed to decline by approximately six per cent annually, whereas existing national climate plans, including conditional commitments, would deliver at best only one-third of the required reductions.
Even if fully implemented, he warned, current national plans would leave the world facing warming of more than 2.5°C by the end of the century, increasing the risk of dangerous and irreversible climate tipping points.
The Secretary-General consequently called for an extraordinary acceleration of climate action, identifying climate justice as a defining challenge of the coming decade.
He expressed concern that developing and emerging economies outside China, despite being home to nearly two-thirds of humanity, receive less than one-fifth of global clean energy investments.
He further noted that many of these countries pay two to three times more to borrow, making it difficult to finance renewable energy infrastructure and climate adaptation programmes.
To address these inequalities, Guterres proposed a new Climate Justice Compact based on shared responsibility, security and benefits, insisting that countries should not be expected to transform their economies without adequate financial and technological support.
He said the compact should rest on four pillars, beginning with accelerating a just transition away from fossil fuels.
Under this approach, he urged governments to develop credible national roadmaps for transitioning away from fossil fuels, protect affected workers and communities, stop approving new coal projects and avoid new oil and gas infrastructure that would undermine the 1.5°C target.
He also called for significant reductions in methane emissions and rapid expansion of renewable energy, electricity grids, energy storage and clean electrification.
Citing findings from the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) Emissions Gap Report, Guterres said global renewable energy capacity must at least triple by 2035 compared with 2025 levels, while unabated coal power must decline by at least 75 per cent.
By 2040, he said, unabated coal power should be almost completely phased out, while oil and gas consumption should fall by approximately one-third.
The second pillar focuses on protecting people against escalating climate impacts.
Guterres called for a new generation of national adaptation plans capable of addressing the consequences of warming beyond 1.5°C, with international support for developing countries.
He stressed the need to ensure that everyone on the planet is covered by an early warning system and that communities are protected against flooding, droughts and rising sea levels.
He also called for swift and accessible support for countries and communities experiencing climate-related losses and damages beyond their capacity to adapt.
On climate finance, the third pillar, the UN chief urged developed countries to deliver at least $300 billion annually by 2035 and establish concrete plans to triple adaptation finance within the same period.
He said the broader $1.3 trillion climate finance goal must translate into actual financial flows to developing countries.
Guterres also called on multilateral development banks to exceed their Baku commitment of providing $120 billion annually by 2030, urging shareholders to empower the institutions to increase lending, mobilise private investments and deploy innovative financing instruments.
He further urged donors to ensure ambitious replenishments of the Green Climate Fund and the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.
The Secretary-General also called for greater South-South cooperation to expand access to climate technologies and finance, while insisting that companies benefiting from fossil fuel production should contribute to addressing the damage caused by their activities.
Making a case for taxing windfall profits from fossil fuel companies, he contrasted the $95 billion earned by the nine largest oil companies in the last quarter alone with the approximately $600 million received by the Loss and Damage Fund.
According to him, the oil companies generated an amount equivalent to the fund’s entire contributions in approximately 14 hours.
“Polluters must pay,” he declared.
The fourth pillar, he said, requires countries to prioritise international cooperation over geopolitical fragmentation, trade barriers and technology monopolies, which could increase the cost of the energy transition and leave vulnerable populations behind.
He stressed that although countries might not agree on every issue, cooperation was essential in areas that no single nation could address independently.
Guterres also urged a shift in the global climate process from negotiations to practical implementation, saying success should increasingly be measured by tangible results on the ground.
He identified electricity grids, critical minerals, methane reduction and early warning systems as areas where international cooperation could deliver significant progress.
The UN chief further acknowledged the contributions of young people, scientists, Indigenous Peoples, civil society organisations and Small Island Developing States to the global climate movement.
Describing them as the conscience of the climate struggle, he praised their efforts to challenge powerful interests, demand faster action and keep public attention focused on the realities of climate change.
Guterres, who disclosed that he would leave office as UN Secretary-General next year, pledged to remain actively involved in the fight against climate change.
He said he would continue advocating for climate action and supporting those working towards a sustainable future, even after completing his tenure.
“I will not stop telling the truth. And I will not stop fighting for it. I will be standing side-by-side with you. As an advocate and an ally,” he said.
He urged world leaders and climate campaigners to sustain pressure for meaningful action, stressing that the opportunity to build cleaner economies, fairer societies and a safer world remained within humanity’s reach.

sources.news_title: UN chief urges world leaders to tackle fossil fuels at COP31 - Turkish Minute
sources.text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Wednesday railed against the oil and gas lobby, telling world leaders fossil fuels “must go the way of the dinosaurs” at a climate summit missing several prominent figures.
The two-week COP31 talks opened in Turkey earlier this week, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change following a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe and deadly floods in Nepal.
“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us,” Guterres told dozens of world leaders gathered in the Mediterranean city of Antalya for two days of speeches by heads of state and government.
But few major breakthroughs are expected at the negotiations, which run until November 20, as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fueled by the US war with Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Since agreeing in 2023, for the first time, to transition away from fossil fuels, the main driver of climate change, countries have struggled to make progress towards that goal at successive annual COP conferences.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” Guterres said, urging governments to tax the windfall profits of oil companies.
“Their strategy is simple: Distort the science. Delay the policy. Delay the action. Delay the accountability. It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil fuel addiction,” he said to sustained applause.
Leaders missing
Guterres, who has made the fight against climate change a central issue since taking office in 2017, is attending his final COP before his term ends in December.
But several prominent figures are absent, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only leader from a G7 country scheduled to address the summit.
“Since the start of this year, climate change has disappeared from speeches and documents from our global leadership,” recently re-elected Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva told fellow leaders.
“We’ve turned to talking more about arms and tariffs than the survival of future generations,” he said.
Climate campaigners breathed a huge sigh of relief when Lula, who has overseen a dramatic drop in deforestation in the Amazon, defeated right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s presidential election last month.
“Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet,” Lula said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is due to attend the meeting, but French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni are skipping it. COP31 coincides with an EU leaders’ summit in Ireland on Thursday.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are also absent from the latest list of expected attendees.
US President Donald Trump, who withdrew the United States from the Paris Agreement and has not sent officials to climate talks since his re-election in 2024, is not attending the summit.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who rarely attends COP meetings, will be represented by Vice President Han Zheng. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is also absent.
The United States and China are the world’s two largest economies and biggest emitters of planet-warming greenhouse gases.
Low expectations
“It is a shame that some of the bigger European leaders aren’t coming. We need Europe to be showing up strongly at this COP,” Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think tank E3G, told Agence France-Presse.
Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s climate commissioner, said the absences were “not completely atypical,” as leaders might have “practical” reasons for being unable to attend a summit.
But he also told reporters in Brussels that “expectations are not necessarily high” for this year’s climate conference.
COP31 host Turkey is promoting a voluntary initiative to accelerate the electrification of transport, buildings and industry, with the aim of increasing electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.
The European Union has stressed that electrification must be “clean,” potentially setting up a debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said the world needs a “fair” energy transition that “takes into account the energy security and different development needs of different countries.”

sources.news_title: UN Chief: Fossil Fuels Must Face Extinction at COP31
sources.text:
The United Nations Secretary-General has warned world leaders at the COP31 summit that the fossil fuel industry must “go the way of the dinosaurs” if the global community is to survive the escalating climate crisis.
The call for a decisive end to the era of carbon-intensive energy was made during the opening of the two-week climate talks in Turkey. Governments are entering negotiations under intense pressure following a year of extreme weather, including searing heatwaves and wildfires across Europe and catastrophic flooding in Nepal.
The statement issued at the start of the COP31 proceedings places immense pressure on petrostates and industrialised nations to accelerate their transition away from coal, oil, and gas.
Economic tensions and the demand for climate finance
The UN Chief’s metaphor suggests that clinging to fossil fuels is no longer a viable survival strategy for the global economy. However, the directive to phase out these energy sources presents a complex dilemma for emerging economies, particularly in Africa.
For nations such as Nigeria, which relies heavily on hydrocarbon exports for national revenue, the transition requires a delicate balance between meeting climate commitments and ensuring economic stability. Many African leaders have argued that any global shift must be a “just transition,” ensuring that developing countries are not left behind as the world moves toward renewables.
A central point of contention at the Turkey summit is the provision of climate finance. Developing nations are calling for significant financial assistance from wealthier, historically high-emitting countries to fund green infrastructure and adapt to the damage already caused by climate change. Without these funds, many argue that the transition will remain an impossible task for the Global South.
Negotiators are expected to focus on the implementation of “loss and damage” funds and the establishment of clear, binding targets for renewable energy investment. The success of the two-week summit depends on whether wealthy nations will commit to the financial frameworks necessary to support the transition in developing economies.
