sources.news_title: Guterres urges countries to cut emissions by 6% annually and speed up shift from fossil fuels
sources.text:
KEY POINTS
- UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for annual global emissions reductions of at least 6 per cent in the coming years.
- He warned that dependence on fossil fuels carries economic and security risks, alongside its contribution to climate change.
- More than 90,000 people are expected at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, as countries face pressure to deliver on climate commitments.
MAIN STORY
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has urged countries to accelerate the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, calling for global emissions to fall by at least 6 per cent annually in the coming years.
Guterres also called for economies that are cleaner, more secure and less vulnerable to external shocks, as delegates gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31).
The UN Deputy Spokesperson, Farhan Haq, disclosed this on Tuesday while briefing UN correspondents in New York, following the secretary-general’s engagements at the conference.
Haq said Guterres addressed the COP30 Presidency Roadmap for Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Energy Systems in a Just, Orderly and Equitable Manner, emphasising the need for countries to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels.
According to the UN chief, fossil fuels are not only driving the climate crisis but also exposing countries to economic and security risks. He pointed to the conflict in the Middle East as an illustration of the consequences of dependence on fossil energy.
Guterres also held bilateral meetings with Türkiye’s President, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and China’s Vice President, Han Zheng, to discuss international cooperation and the expected outcomes of COP31.
During his meeting with Erdoğan, they discussed climate action and cooperation at the summit, alongside regional and international issues including the war in Ukraine, the Middle East conflict, Libya and Cyprus.
His discussion with Han focused on the need for credible COP31 outcomes that address gaps in emissions reduction, climate finance and adaptation.
The secretary-general also met members of the Youth Advisory Group and participated in a roundtable with young people. He said young people should be recognised as active participants and leaders in climate discussions, rather than simply beneficiaries of climate policies.
He urged them to connect international climate negotiations with their communities and help communicate scientific information online, where climate disinformation can spread rapidly.
Guterres further met climate scientists to discuss recent developments in climate science, financing and the energy transition, as well as policy priorities for the conference and beyond.
More than 90,000 people are expected to attend COP31, which opened on Monday and is scheduled to close on November 20.
THE ISSUES
Guterres’ call for annual emissions cuts of at least 6 per cent reflects the pressure on governments to move beyond climate promises and reduce the amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere.
The fossil fuel issue is also an economic concern. Countries that depend heavily on oil and gas can face higher energy costs and supply disruptions when conflicts affect production, transportation or international trade. The Middle East crisis has brought this vulnerability into focus, showing how instability in one region can affect energy markets elsewhere.
For Nigeria, the transition presents a difficult balance. Oil and gas remain important sources of government revenue and foreign exchange, while the country also faces the need to expand reliable electricity supply and reduce exposure to costly energy imports. Moving towards renewable energy therefore involves more than setting emissions targets. It requires investment in power infrastructure, financing, technology and reliable alternatives that businesses and households can afford.
The emphasis on climate finance and adaptation is equally important. Countries need funding not only to develop cleaner energy systems but also to prepare for the effects of climate change, including damage to agriculture, infrastructure and livelihoods. Without adequate financing, developing economies may struggle to meet emissions targets while addressing immediate development needs.
Guterres’ engagement with young people and climate scientists also highlights another challenge facing climate negotiations: translating scientific evidence and international agreements into public understanding and practical action. Climate commitments have limited value if communities do not understand the changes required or governments fail to implement them.
WHAT’S NEXT
COP31 is expected to continue until November 20, with negotiations focused on strengthening cooperation and securing outcomes on emissions reduction, climate finance and adaptation.
The challenge for participating countries will be to turn their commitments into measurable action, particularly on reducing fossil fuel dependence and supporting economies that face the highest costs of climate change.
BOTTOM LINE
Guterres is pressing governments to treat the energy transition as both a climate priority and an economic security issue. The outcome of COP31 will be measured not only by the promises made in Antalya but by whether countries can translate them into faster emissions cuts, cleaner energy systems and practical support for vulnerable economies.

sources.news_title: EU urged to 'show leadership' at COP31
sources.text:
COP31
EU urged to 'show leadership' at COP31
Greens MEPs say they are pessimistic about the prospects of the latest global climate event yielding any firm results. Michael Bloss and Kai Tegethoff were speaking in Brussels as world leaders and negotiators gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31. Both agree that Antalya will be a crucial moment for the world to move forward on the phase-out of fossil fuels, at a time when record heatwaves, floods and wildfires show the climate crisis is already here. The EU’s role will be essential in securing global momentum in the fight against climate change, they say. But, speaking to this website before leaving for the talks, Bloss said he had little hope that two of the three things he hoped the conference might produce will actually happen.
The two are, he said, a greater commitment to phasing out fossil fuels and, secondly, encouraging the EU to come up with more financing for tackling climate change. Bloss, who will be attending his 8th COP conference, said, “I expect nothing I have to say on these two things, especially without the US at the table” The only positive outcome he foresees, he said, is on renewable-based electrification. He is critical of the role of the EU on climate issues, saying it is guilty of providing “too little leadership”.
“The idea of a rules based order is being challenged like never before and the EU is right, of course, in defending it (rules based).But climate issues are central to this and the EU needs to provide more leadership in slowing the climate crisis. At present, I do not see that happening,” he said. He pointed out that this was all the more necessary as Europe, in recent years, had been the “one continent in the world” that is experiencing climate change at its most acute. Despite reservations in some quarters, he still believes the COP events have a role to play.
He said: “Yes, there are things may be more fit for purpose but, even so, I still think we would be worse off without it (COP).” His comments are partly echoed by his group colleague Kai Tegethoff, also a German MEP, who will also attend the talks and told this site he expects COP31 to focus on electrification, saying: “I do understand the reasons for that.” But he also hopes the conference will “still talk about” other issues, particularly phasing out fossil fuels and climate adaptation.
He too looks to the EU for more of a leadership role in the talks, saying, “It has lost this a bit but its role is to be demanding on the global stage. The question is: Is is ready to act?” He is particularly scathing of the principle of unanimity at the COP talks. At the event the long-standing rule of unanimity (consensus) is facing severe scrutiny and active circumvention by frustrated nations. Under the standard United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) rules, formal decisions require consensus among all 198 parties, meaning a single objecting country can stall or veto global progress.
The MEP says that while this needs reforming he still believes the COP conference is a “valuable” chance for all parties to “come together and to see where we land”. Speaking separately, Ciarán Cuffe, Co-Chair of the European Green Party, said: “With the US federal government once again absent from the climate negotiations, Europe must lead the global transition.” Vula Tsetsi, Co-Chair of the European Green Party, said: “The EU cannot claim to be a global leader on climate change while weakening the European Green Deal and rolling back its own commitments. Europe must lead by example, ending public subsidies for fossil fuels and building a coalition for a fossil-free future.”
